grammarItems.title: Hangul syllable blocks
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Korean is written in syllable blocks. Each block usually has an initial consonant, a vowel, and sometimes a final consonant.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Study this before memorizing many words so you can read Korean from Hangul instead of depending on romanization.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Read each block left-to-right or top-to-bottom inside the square: 한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ, 글 = ㄱ + ㅡ + ㄹ.
grammarItems.contrastWith: Romanization is only a temporary pronunciation helper. It is not the real Korean spelling.

examples.en: Hangul / Korean writing
I eat.
I listen.

commonMistakes: Do not pronounce romanization as English spelling.
Do not pause between every syllable block when speaking.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean doesn't write letters in a straight line like English; instead it packs them into square syllable blocks, each holding one initial consonant, one vowel, and an optional final consonant (the 받침). Think of every block as one beat you say out loud: 한 is ㅎ+ㅏ+ㄴ, and 글 is ㄱ+ㅡ+ㄹ, so 한글 is just two beats. The vowel sits to the right of the initial (가) or underneath it (고), depending on the vowel's shape. The common beginner trap is trying to read the letters left-to-right across the whole word; always group them into blocks first, or words like 학교 become unreadable.

grammarItems.title: Topic and contrast
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say what the sentence is about: “as for...” or “when we talk about this...”
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 은/는 when introducing yourself, setting the topic, comparing two things, or changing the topic.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 은 after a final consonant and 는 after a vowel: 학생은, 저는.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 이/가 points to the subject or new information. 은/는 sets the topic or contrast.

examples.en: As for me, I am a student.
As for today, I cannot go.
What is this?

commonMistakes: Do not translate 은/는 every time. It often just marks the topic.
Do not stack 도 after 은/는 as 저는도; say 저도.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 은/는 attaches to a noun to mark it as the topic, the thing the rest of the sentence is about, roughly like saying 'as for...' in English. Picture it as spotlighting one item and quietly comparing it to others: 저는 학생이에요 means 'as for me, I'm a student,' often hinting 'others might not be.' Use 은 after a final consonant (선생님은) and 는 after a vowel (저는). Beginners overuse it as a plain subject marker, but if you're introducing brand-new information or answering 'who did it?', you usually want 이/가 instead.

grammarItems.title: Subject and new information
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to mark the subject that exists, appears, hurts, or is being identified.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 이/가 with 있어요, 없어요, 아파요, 좋아요, and when the subject is new or important.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 이 after a final consonant and 가 after a vowel: 시간이, 친구가.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 은/는 is the topic. 이/가 points to the subject inside the sentence.

examples.en: I have time. / There is time.
A friend is coming.
My head hurts.

commonMistakes: Do not use 을/를 with 있어요 or 없어요 for the thing that exists.
Memorize common chunks first: 시간이 있어요, 문제가 없어요, 머리가 아파요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 이/가 marks the grammatical subject, especially when something newly appears, exists, happens to you, or is the specific answer to a question. The intuition: 이/가 points a finger and says 'this one, right here,' while 은/는 steps back to set a theme. For example 비가 와요 ('rain is coming') and 누가 왔어요? — 친구가 왔어요 ('who came? a friend came') both spotlight fresh, specific information. Use 이 after a consonant (책이) and 가 after a vowel (친구가); a frequent slip is saying 저가 instead of the irregular 제가 for 'I.'

grammarItems.title: Object marker
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this after the thing that receives the action.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 을/를 with verbs like eat, drink, buy, read, write, study, watch, and take.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 을 after a final consonant and 를 after a vowel: 밥을, 커피를.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 이/가 marks the subject. 을/를 marks the object of an action.

examples.en: I eat rice / a meal.
I drink coffee.
I study Korean.

commonMistakes: Koreans often drop 을/를 in speech, but learners should understand it first.
Do not put 을/를 after places with 가요; say 학교에 가요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 을/를 marks the direct object, the thing that directly receives the action of the verb, answering 'what?' or 'whom?' after a verb. A handy mental model: the object is whatever the verb is 'done to,' so in 물을 마셔요 ('I drink water'), 물 is being drunk. Attach 을 after a final consonant (밥을 먹어요) and 를 after a vowel (커피를 마셔요). In casual speech Koreans often drop this particle entirely (밥 먹어요), so don't panic when you don't hear it, but in writing and clear sentences it's the reliable signal of what's being acted on.

grammarItems.title: Time, destination, and existence place
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for “to,” “at,” “in,” or “on” when the noun is a destination, time, or place where something exists.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에 with 가요/와요 for destination, with times like 7시에, and with 있어요/없어요 for location.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 에 directly after the noun: 학교에, 집에, 7시에.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에서 is where an action happens. 에 is the destination or existence location.

examples.en: I go to school.
I wake up at seven.
I am at home.

commonMistakes: For destination, use 에: 학교에 가요.
For the place of an action, use 에서: 학교에서 공부해요.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에 is a quiet, all-purpose particle for time, a destination you're heading to, and the location where something simply exists. Think of it as pinning a noun to a point on a map or a clock: 학교에 가요 ('I go to school'), 세 시에 만나요 ('let's meet at three'), and 집에 있어요 ('I'm at home'). Notice it marks where something is, not where an action busily happens. The classic mistake is using 에 for the place of an action like eating or studying; for that you need 에서, so 도서관에 공부해요 is wrong and 도서관에서 공부해요 is right.

grammarItems.title: Action place and starting point
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for the place where an action happens, or the place something starts from.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에서 with study, work, eat, wait, buy, meet, and with came from.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 에서 after the place: 학교에서, 회사에서, 서울에서.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에 is destination or existence place. 에서 is action place.

examples.en: I study at school.
I work at a company.
I came from Seoul.

commonMistakes: Do not say 학교에서 가요 for destination. Say 학교에 가요.
Use 에서 only when an action is happening there or something starts there.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에서 marks the place where an action actively takes place, and it also means 'from' a starting point. The intuition: if a verb shows real activity happening somewhere, that location takes 에서, as in 카페에서 일해요 ('I work at the cafe') or 식당에서 먹어요 ('I eat at the restaurant'). For the 'from' sense, it shows origin: 한국에서 왔어요 ('I came from Korea'). The key beginner confusion is 에 versus 에서; remember that still existence (있다, 살다 sometimes) tends toward 에, while busy actions take 에서, so you sit 의자에 but study 도서관에서.

grammarItems.title: To a person
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this when a person receives an item, message, action, or question.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 에게 in neutral/written Korean, 한테 in everyday speech, and 께 for honorific speech.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach directly after the person: 친구에게, 저한테, 선생님께.
grammarItems.contrastWith: Use 에 for places. Use 에게/한테 for people or animals.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: Who do I give it to?

examples.en: I give a gift to a friend.
Please give me the receipt.
I ask the teacher.

commonMistakes: Do not use 에게 for ordinary destinations. Say 학교에 가요, not 학교에게 가요.
Use 께 with respected people when you want honorific direction.

practiceItems.prompt: I give a gift to a friend.

grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 에게/한테 marks the person (or animal) who receives something, like a gift, a message, or an action directed at them, matching English 'to' someone. Picture an arrow flying toward a recipient: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요 ('I gave a present to my friend') or 엄마한테 전화했어요 ('I called mom'). The two are interchangeable in meaning, but 한테 sounds casual and conversational while 에게 feels a bit more formal or written. Two cautions for beginners: don't use these for places (a destination still takes 에, not 에게), and when speaking to someone you must respect, switch to the honorific form 께 instead.

grammarItems.title: Method, direction, and language
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this for by, with, toward, or in a language.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 로/으로 for transportation, payment, tools, direction, and language.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ ending. Use 으로 after most consonants: 카드로, 펜으로.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 을/를 marks the object. 로/으로 marks the method or tool.

examples.en: Can I pay by card?
I speak in Korean.
I go by subway.

commonMistakes: 카드로 사요 means buy by card, not buy a card.
Do not use 로/으로 for “with a friend”; use 친구하고 or 친구랑 for that meaning.
Do not confuse 로/으로 with destination 에.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: This particle marks the means, method, or direction of an action, and also the language something is spoken in. A handy mental model: attach it to a noun and think "by means of / toward / using" that noun. Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로 가요 = I go by bus; 집으로 = toward home) and 으로 after other consonants; for language, 한국어로 말해요 = I speak in Korean. The classic pitfall is confusing it with 에 (a fixed destination)—로/으로 stresses the route or tool, not the final spot itself.

grammarItems.title: Also / too / even
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to add one more thing to the same idea.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 도 for me too, this too, today too, and similar additions.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 도 after the word you are adding: 저도, 이것도, 오늘도.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 도 often replaces 은/는, 이/가, or 을/를 in that position.

examples.en: I am going too.
This too, please.
I study today too.

commonMistakes: Say 저도, not 저는도.
도 changes focus, so place it after the exact word you are adding.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 도 means "also," "too," or even "even," piling one more item onto what was already mentioned. Picture stacking things on a tray: whatever 도 attaches to gets added to the list. Crucially, 도 replaces the subject/topic and object particles—so you say 저도 학생이에요 (I'm a student too), never 저는도. Another example: 커피도 좋아요 = I like coffee too. The common beginner slip is keeping 은/는 or 이/가 in front of 도; just drop them and let 도 do the work.

grammarItems.title: Only / just
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use this to limit the sentence to one thing.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 만 for only this, only water, only today, or just one thing.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Attach 만 after the word you want to limit: 물만, 오늘만, 이것만.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 도 adds another thing. 만 limits the sentence to one thing.

examples.en: I only drink water.
I rest only today.
Only this, please.

commonMistakes: 만 changes focus. 물만 마셔요 means only water, not only drinking.
Place 만 after the word you want to limit.
grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: 만 means "only" or "just," narrowing your statement down to one thing and excluding everything else. Think of it as drawing a tight circle around a single noun: nothing else counts. For example 물만 마셔요 = I drink only water, and 한 명만 왔어요 = only one person came. Unlike 도, 만 can sit with some particles (학교에서만 = only at school), but a frequent mistake is forcing 이/가 or 을/를 after it; usually 만 just replaces them, as in 이것만 주세요 = give me just this.

grammarItems.title: From / until
grammarItems.plainEnglish: Use these to mark the start and end of a time or place range.
grammarItems.whenToUse: Use 부터/까지 with schedules, opening hours, travel routes, and time ranges.
grammarItems.attachmentRule: Use 부터 for the start and 까지 for the end: 9시부터 6시까지.
grammarItems.contrastWith: 에 marks one time or place. 부터/까지 marks a range.

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: From what time do you work?

miniDialogue.speaker: A
miniDialogue.en: I walk from here to the station.

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
I study from Monday to Friday.
I walk from here to the station.

commonMistakes: 까지 can mean until for time or as far as for place.
Do not use only 부터 if the ending point is important.

practiceItems.prompt: I walk from here to the station.

grammarItems.beginnerExplanation: This pair marks the start and end of a range: 부터 means "from" (a beginning point) and 까지 means "until/to" (an ending point), for both time and place. Imagine drawing a line with a starting dot and a finishing dot. A natural sentence is 아침부터 저녁까지 일해요 = I work from morning until evening. Note that for a starting *place* Korean usually prefers 에서 over 부터 (집에서 학교까지 = from home to school), so the pitfall is overusing 부터 for physical locations.

endingItems.title: Want to do
endingItems.plainEnglish: Add 고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for your own wants: eating, going, resting, learning, buying, or trying something.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the dictionary form, then add 고 싶어요: 먹다 → 먹고 싶어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Use N 주세요 to ask for an item. Use V고 싶어요 to talk about your desire.

examples.en: I want to drink coffee.
I want to go home.
I want to rest today.

commonMistakes: Do not use 고 싶어요 for adjectives like pretty or expensive.
For another person's wants, beginners can first quote or ask directly instead of overbuilding grammar.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: To say you want to do something, take a verb stem and add 고 싶어요. Mental model: 고 glues onto the action and 싶어요 adds the feeling of "I wish to." For example 먹다 (to eat) becomes 먹고 싶어요 = I want to eat, and 가다 becomes 가고 싶어요 = I want to go. Two pitfalls: this is for *your own* desire with action verbs, not for "I want a thing" (use 원해요 or 필요해요 for nouns), and when talking about someone else's want you switch to 고 싶어해요.

endingItems.title: Can do / possible
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say an action is possible because of skill, time, permission-like possibility, or circumstances.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for ability and practical possibility: can go, can eat, can read, can pay by card.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use ㄹ 수 있어요 after a vowel-ending stem and 을 수 있어요 after a consonant-ending stem.
endingItems.contrastWith: 못 + verb is the shorter everyday way to say cannot.

examples.en: I can go today.
I can read Hangul.
Can I pay by card?

commonMistakes: Do not use this for simple preference; use 고 싶어요 for want.
For quick speech, 카드 돼요? is a natural shortcut in stores.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending expresses ability or possibility—"can" or "it's possible to." Attach ㄹ 수 있어요 to a stem ending in a vowel and 을 수 있어요 to one ending in a consonant; literally 수 means a "way/method" that 있어요 (exists). For example 할 수 있어요 = I can do it, and 먹을 수 있어요 = I can eat it. To say you can't, flip 있어요 to 없어요 (갈 수 없어요 = I can't go); the common slip is forgetting the space before 수 or mixing up the ㄹ/을 choice.

endingItems.title: Cannot / unable to
endingItems.plainEnglish: Put 못 before a verb to say you cannot do it because of ability, schedule, rules, health, or circumstances.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for real limits: schedule conflicts, food restrictions, language ability, health, rules, or practical impossibility.
endingItems.attachmentRule: For most verbs, put 못 before the normal polite verb. For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun + 못 해요.
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 means you do not do something. 못 means you cannot do it.

examples.en: I cannot go today.
I cannot eat spicy food.
I cannot speak Korean well.

commonMistakes: Say 못 가요, not 못 가해요.
For 하다 verbs, use 못 해요 or noun + 못 해요: 공부 못 해요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 못 goes right before a verb to say you *can't* do something because of a circumstance, lack of skill, or outside obstacle—not because you choose not to. Think of it as a wall blocking the action even though you might want to do it. For example 못 가요 = I can't go (something prevents me), and 수영 못 해요 = I can't swim. Don't confuse 못 with 안, which means you simply *don't* by choice (안 가요 = I'm not going); also note 하다 verbs split, so it's 수영 못 해요, not 못 수영해요.

endingItems.title: Have to / must
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to say an action is necessary or required.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for schedules, rules, health needs, work, school, and personal obligations.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 야 해요: 가다 → 가야 해요, 먹다 → 먹어야 해요.
endingItems.contrastWith: V지 않아도 돼요 means the action is not necessary.

examples.en: I have to go early tomorrow.
I have to take medicine.
I have a test, so I have to study.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for a simple future plan; it sounds like obligation.
하다 verbs become 해야 해요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending expresses necessity or obligation — the English "have to" or "must." Picture it as two ideas glued together: "if I do this action, then it's good/okay," so doing the thing is the only acceptable path. For example, 약을 먹어야 해요 means "I have to take my medicine," and 집에 가야 해요 means "I have to go home." A common beginner slip is forgetting the vowel harmony on the stem (가 + 아야 → 가야, not 가어야), and remember that for permission you switch to 아/어도 돼요, not this form.

endingItems.title: May I / is it okay to do?
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to ask whether an action is allowed or okay.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it before sitting, entering, taking photos, using a card, or doing anything where permission matters.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 도 돼요?
endingItems.contrastWith: V지 마세요 tells someone not to do something.

examples.en: May I sit here?
May I take a photo?
Can I use a card?

commonMistakes: Use a question intonation when asking permission.
Do not confuse 돼요 with 되어요 spelling; 돼요 is the common form.

practiceItems.prompt: 사진 찍다 → may I take a photo?
카드 쓰다 → may I use a card?

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Use this to ask for or grant permission — "May I?" or "Is it okay if I...?" The intuition is "even if I do this action, it still turns out fine," so the 도 carries an "even" nuance and 돼요 means "it works / it's okay." You might ask 여기 앉아도 돼요? ("May I sit here?") and hear back 네, 앉아도 돼요 ("Yes, you may sit"). Beginners often confuse this with obligation: 가야 해요 means "I have to go," while 가도 돼요 means "I may go," so don't mix up 야 해요 and 도 돼요.

endingItems.title: Please do
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to politely ask someone to do an action.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for help, opening, repeating, taking a photo, checking something, or saying something again.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use the 아/어 form of the verb, then add 주세요.
endingItems.contrastWith: N 주세요 asks for an item. V아/어 주세요 asks someone to do an action.

examples.en: Please help me.
Please say it again.
Please open the door.

commonMistakes: Do not use this for your own action; it asks someone else to act.
Add 좀 to soften many everyday requests.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is how you politely ask someone to do something for you — "please do (it)." Think of 주세요 as literally "please give me," so you are asking the listener to "give" you the favor of the action. For instance, 잠깐만 기다려 주세요 means "please wait a moment," and 천천히 말해 주세요 means "please speak slowly." Don't confuse this with 주세요 attached to a noun (물 주세요, "water please"); the 아/어 주세요 form needs a verb stem, and avoid it for prohibitions — "please don't" uses 지 마세요 instead.

endingItems.title: Please do not
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this for polite prohibitions, warnings, signs, and careful requests.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when telling someone not to go, not to take photos, not to open something, or not to worry.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the dictionary form, then add 지 마세요.
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 V해요 says someone does not do an action. V지 마세요 tells someone not to do it.

examples.en: Please do not take photos here.
Please do not go yet.
Please do not worry.

commonMistakes: This can sound like an instruction, so use it carefully with people.
You will often read it on signs before you need to say it yourself.

practiceItems.prompt: 사진 찍다 → please do not take photos

endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending tells someone politely NOT to do an action — you'll see it on signs and hear it from staff. Mentally, 지 마세요 attaches the "stop/don't" verb 말다 to any action, like putting a red circle over a picture. Common examples are 만지지 마세요 ("please don't touch") and 사진을 찍지 마세요 ("please don't take photos"). A frequent mistake is trying to negate with 안 here — you can't say 안 만지세요 for a command; prohibitions specifically use the 지 마세요 pattern, and note the stem keeps its 지 with no vowel harmony.

endingItems.title: Because / so
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this to connect a reason to a result.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for simple reasons: busy so cannot go, sick so rest, expensive so do not buy.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use 아서 after many ㅏ/ㅗ stems and 어서 after many other stems. 하다 becomes 해서.
endingItems.contrastWith: 고 simply connects ideas; 아서/어서 explains why.

examples.en: I am busy, so I cannot go.
I am sick, so I rest.
Sorry I am late.

commonMistakes: Avoid using 아서/어서 before commands in careful textbook grammar.
Keep the first clause short as a beginner.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This connector links a reason to its result — "because" or "so." Imagine the first clause naturally flowing downhill into the second: the cause comes first, then the effect, with no tense marking on the 아서/어서 part itself. For example, 배가 고파서 밥을 먹었어요 means "I was hungry, so I ate," and 비가 와서 집에 있었어요 means "because it rained, I stayed home." The big pitfall: never use 아서/어서 with commands or suggestions (don't say 피곤해서 쉬세요) — for those reasons you need 으니까 instead.

endingItems.title: And / and then
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use 고 to connect two actions or descriptions.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for sequence or listing: eat and go, study and work, cheap and good.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the first verb or adjective, then add 고.
endingItems.contrastWith: 아서/어서 gives a reason. 고 usually just connects.

examples.en: I eat and go to school.
I study and work.
This bag is cheap and good.

commonMistakes: 고 does not always mean a strict time order; context decides.
Do not make beginner sentences too long.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This connector strings actions or descriptions together — "and" or "and then." Think of 고 as a simple chain link: it can list qualities at the same time (이 방은 크고 밝아요, "this room is big and bright") or put events in sequence (밥을 먹고 학교에 갔어요, "I ate and then went to school"). The key intuition is that 고 stays plain — you don't conjugate tense on it; the final verb carries the tense for the whole sentence. Beginners sometimes reach for 고 to mean "because"; for cause-and-effect you want 아서/어서 instead.

endingItems.title: If / when
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use 면 to set a condition.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for time, price, health, permission, and simple advice.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Remove 다 from the verb or adjective, then add 면.
endingItems.contrastWith: 아서/어서 gives a reason that already exists. 면 gives a condition.

examples.en: If you have time, please call.
If it is expensive, I do not buy it.
If you are sick, you should rest.

commonMistakes: Context can make 면 sound like if or when.
Keep the condition short at first.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Attach 면 (or 으면 after a consonant) to set up a condition — "if" or "when." The mental model is a doorway: "once this first situation happens, the second part follows." For example, 시간이 있으면 만나요 means "if you have time, let's meet," and 봄이 오면 꽃이 펴요 means "when spring comes, flowers bloom." Note that Korean uses one 면 for both "if" and "when," so context decides; a common slip is forgetting the 으 after a consonant stem (먹다 → 먹으면, not 먹면).

endingItems.title: I will / speaker promise
endingItems.plainEnglish: Use this when the speaker decides or promises what they will do.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when volunteering, responding to someone, leaving, waiting, or promising a call.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use ㄹ게요 after a vowel-ending stem and 을게요 after a consonant-ending stem.
endingItems.contrastWith: ㄹ/을 거예요 is a future plan. ㄹ/을게요 is the speaker's decision in response to the situation.

examples.en: I will do it.
I will wait here.
I will call later.

commonMistakes: Use this only for what the speaker will do.
Do not use it to predict another person's action.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This ending voices the speaker's own decision or promise — "I will (do it)." The crucial intuition is that it's a commitment made to the listener, often reacting to them, not a neutral forecast about the future. For example, 제가 할게요 means "I'll do it (so don't worry)," and 내일 전화할게요 means "I'll call you tomorrow (I promise)." The classic pitfall is using it for other people or for predictions — you can't say 비가 올게요 for "it will rain"; 을게요 only works with first-person "I," and for plain predictions use 을 거예요 instead.

endingItems.title: Describing a noun: now vs later
endingItems.plainEnglish: Put a describing word in front of a noun. The ㄴ/은 form says how something is right now; the ㄹ/을 form says how it will or might be.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it whenever a describing word comes before a noun: 뜨거운 물 (hot water), 큰 가방 (a big bag), 매운 음식 (spicy food).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Adjective + ㄴ after a vowel (크다 → 큰), 은 after a consonant (작다 → 작은). ㅂ-irregulars become 운 (맵다 → 매운, 쉽다 → 쉬운); 있다/없다 use 는 (맛있다 → 맛있는). For the will/might sense, use ㄹ after a vowel and 을 after a consonant (뜨거울, 작을).
endingItems.contrastWith: 뜨거운 물 = water that is hot right now; 뜨거울 물 = water that will become hot. Same adjective, different time feeling.

examples.en: Please give me hot water.
It is a small room.
I like spicy food.
It is delicious coffee.

commonMistakes: Don't use the ㄹ/을 form for present description: it is 뜨거운 물 (hot now), not 뜨거울 물, when the water is hot right now.
ㅂ-irregular adjectives change to 운: 맵다 → 매운 (not 맵은), 쉽다 → 쉬운.
studyOrder: Pick the adjective and the noun it describes.
Choose the ㄴ/은 form for how it is now.
Apply the ㅂ-irregular (운) or 있다 (는) change if needed.
Use ㄹ/을 only when you mean it will or might be that way.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a describing word sits in front of a noun, Korean changes its ending. The ㄴ/은 form describes how something is right now: 큰 가방 (a big bag), 작은 방 (a small room), 매운 음식 (spicy food). The intuition is a snapshot of the present — so 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot at this moment. Switch to the ㄹ/을 form only for something that will or might become that way later, which is why 뜨거울 물 (water that will get hot) feels different from 뜨거운 물. Watch two traps: ㅂ-irregular adjectives use 운 (맵다 → 매운, not 맵은), and 있다/없다 words use 는 (맛있다 → 맛있는).

endingItems.title: When the stem changes
endingItems.plainEnglish: Some stems reshape their last letter before a vowel ending. Learn the polite form as the anchor and the rest follows.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to understand why 맵다 becomes 매워요, 듣다 becomes 들어요, 크다 becomes 커요, and 살다 becomes 삽니다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel (맵다 → 매워요, 매운); ㄷ → ㄹ before a vowel (듣다 → 들어요); ㅡ drops before 아/어 (크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다, 사는).
endingItems.contrastWith: Regular stems just add the ending (먹다 → 먹어요). Irregular stems change the last letter first, so don't build them literally (not 맵어요, not 듣어요).

examples.en: The soup is spicy.
I listen to the radio.
(Someone) is tall.
I live in Seoul.

commonMistakes: Don't conjugate irregular stems literally: 맵다 → 매워요 (not 맵어요), 듣다 → 들어요 (not 듣어요).
The change only happens before a vowel ending; before a consonant the stem stays (듣고, 듣습니다).
studyOrder: Spot the irregular marker on the card (ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅡ/ㄹ).
Memorize the polite form as the anchor.
Apply the change only before a vowel ending.
Keep the plain stem before consonant endings.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Most Korean stems just take an ending (먹다 → 먹어요), but a few reshape their last letter before a vowel ending, and that surprises beginners. Four common ones: ㅂ becomes 우 (맵다 → 매워요, 매운), ㄷ becomes ㄹ (듣다 → 들어요), ㅡ simply drops before 아/어 (크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요), and ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다, 사는). The safe strategy is to memorize the polite -아/어요 form as your anchor and build outward from it. The change only happens before a vowel ending — before a consonant the stem stays put (듣고, 듣습니다) — so never conjugate them literally as 맵어요 or 듣어요.

endingItems.title: Past Tense
endingItems.plainEnglish: Shows that an action or state already happened or is finished.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to talk about completed past actions or past states, e.g. 어제 영화를 봤어요 (I watched a movie yesterday).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요 (가다→갔어요, 좋다→좋았어요). Otherwise add 었어요 (먹다→먹었어요, 마시다→마셨어요). 하다 verbs become 했어요 (공부하다→공부했어요). Irregular stems shift: ㄷ irregular 듣다→들었어요, ㅂ irregular 춥다→추웠어요, ㅡ drops 바쁘다→바빴어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with present V-아/어요 (지금 먹어요 = I am eating now) versus past V-았/었어요 (아까 먹었어요 = I ate earlier).

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate bread in the morning.
I studied Korean over the weekend.
The weather was really cold yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using 았어요 after a non ㅏ/ㅗ vowel, like saying 먹았어요 instead of the correct 먹었어요.
Saying 하았어요 instead of the contracted irregular form 했어요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ
Add 았어요 or 었어요, or use 했어요 for 하다
Apply irregular changes if the stem is irregular
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The past tense in Korean is built right onto the verb stem, and the only real choice is whether to add 았어요 or 었어요. Listen to the last vowel of the stem: if it is the bright ㅏ or ㅗ sound, you use 았어요, so 가다 becomes 갔어요 (I went) and 좋다 becomes 좋았어요 (it was good). For every other vowel you use 었어요, so 먹다 becomes 먹었어요 (I ate). The single most common pitfall is forgetting that 하다 does not follow the simple pattern; it always becomes 했어요, never 하았어요. Once vowel harmony feels automatic, the past tense becomes one of the easiest endings in Korean.

endingItems.title: Future / Intention
endingItems.plainEnglish: Expresses a future plan, an intention, or a guess about what will happen.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for plans, decisions, or probability, e.g. 내일 영화를 볼 거예요 (I will watch a movie tomorrow).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. After a vowel-ending stem add ㄹ 거예요 (가다→갈 거예요, 보다→볼 거예요). After a consonant-ending stem add 을 거예요 (먹다→먹을 거예요, 읽다→읽을 거예요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ and take ㄹ 거예요 (살다→살 거예요). ㅂ irregular: 돕다→도울 거예요; ㄷ irregular: 듣다→들을 거예요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with present V-아/어요 for current action, and with V-(으)ㄹ게요 which promises something directly to the listener rather than stating a neutral plan.

examples.en: I will go to Busan tomorrow.
I will read a book in the evening.
I will meet a friend on the weekend.
It will probably rain tomorrow.

commonMistakes: Adding 을 거예요 after a vowel stem, like saying 갈을 거예요 instead of 갈 거예요.
Writing 거에요 instead of the correct 거예요.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Check if the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant
Add ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel or 을 거예요 after a consonant
Handle ㄹ-stems and irregular stems
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is the everyday way to talk about the future and about your plans, and it also softens into a guess when you are not certain. The form splits by sound: vowel-ending stems take ㄹ 거예요, so 가다 becomes 갈 거예요 (I will go), while consonant-ending stems take 을 거예요, so 먹다 becomes 먹을 거예요 (I will eat). When you add 아마 (probably) in front, the same ending now means a prediction, as in 아마 비가 올 거예요 (it will probably rain). The biggest beginner pitfall is spelling: it is 거예요, not 거에요, even though they sound almost identical.

endingItems.title: Progressive (be ~ing)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Shows that an action is happening right now and is still going on.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for actions in progress at the moment of speaking, e.g. 지금 밥을 먹고 있어요 (I am eating now).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Simply attach 고 있어요 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change at all; the stem ending in a vowel or a consonant makes no difference (가다→가고 있어요, 먹다→먹고 있어요, 공부하다→공부하고 있어요). For respect toward the subject, 있어요 becomes 계세요 (기다리고 계세요).
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with the simple present V-아/어요, which can state a habit or a general fact, while V-고 있어요 stresses that the action is unfolding right now.

examples.en: I am studying Korean right now.
My younger sibling is listening to music.
Mom is cooking in the kitchen.
I am waiting for a friend.

commonMistakes: Changing the stem vowel before 고, like saying 먹어고 있어요 instead of the correct 먹고 있어요.
Using the plain present 먹어요 when you specifically mean an action in progress right now.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Attach 고 with no vowel change
Add 있어요 to mean is in progress
Switch 있어요 to 계세요 to respect the subject
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-고 있어요 is the Korean equivalent of the English be ~ing, and the good news is that it never changes shape with the verb. You just glue 고 있어요 onto the stem: 먹다 becomes 먹고 있어요 (I am eating) and 가다 becomes 가고 있어요 (I am going), with no vowel harmony to worry about. The reason it matters is contrast: 먹어요 alone can mean I eat in general, but 먹고 있어요 pins the action to this very moment. The classic mistake is reflexively adding 어/아 before 고, producing forms like 먹어고; remember that 고 attaches straight to the bare stem.

endingItems.title: Try Doing
endingItems.plainEnglish: Means to try doing something or to give something a go.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to suggest someone try an action, or to say you experienced trying it, e.g. 이거 한번 먹어 보세요 (Please try eating this).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the 아/어 connective like in present tense. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use 아 보다 (가다→가 보다, 찾다→찾아 보다); otherwise use 어 보다 (먹다→먹어 보다, 입다→입어 보다). 하다 becomes 해 보다. Then conjugate 보다 normally: 보세요 (please try), 봤어요 (tried), 볼 거예요 (will try).
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with the plain action verb: 먹어요 just means eat, while 먹어 봐요 means give eating it a try or eat it and see.

examples.en: Please try eating this kimchi.
I have tried going to Jeju Island.
Please try on these clothes.

examples.ko: 다음에 한국 음식을 만들어 볼 거예요.
examples.romanization: daeume hanguk eumsigeul mandeureo bol geoyeyo.
examples.en: Next time I will try making Korean food.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong connective vowel, like saying 먹아 보세요 instead of the correct 먹어 보세요.
Forgetting to conjugate 보다, leaving it as 먹어 보 instead of 먹어 보세요.
studyOrder: Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Attach 보다 after the connective
Conjugate 보다 for the tense you need
Use 보세요 to gently suggest trying
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 보다 adds the meaning of trying or experiencing on top of any action verb, and it is built from the same 아/어 connective you already use for the present tense. So 먹다 becomes 먹어 보다 (try eating) and 가다 becomes 가 보다 (try going); from there you conjugate the 보다 part freely. In the present polite suggestion 먹어 보세요 it means please give it a try, while in the past 가 봤어요 it means I have tried going, which is a natural way to talk about experiences. The most common slip is leaving 보다 unconjugated, so always finish the ending, as in 보세요 or 봤어요, rather than stopping at 보.

endingItems.title: Mild Surprise
endingItems.plainEnglish: Expresses mild surprise or a fresh realization about something you just noticed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you react to something you just saw, heard, or discovered, e.g. 날씨가 정말 좋네요 (Wow, the weather is really nice).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 네요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (좋다→좋네요, 가다→가네요, 크다→크네요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ before 네요 (멀다→머네요, 살다→사네요). For past reactions use 았/었네요 (왔네요, 먹었네요).
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with the plain statement A/V-아/어요, which simply reports a fact, while A/V-네요 adds the speaker fresh emotional reaction of noticing it now.

examples.en: Wow, you speak Korean really well.
The weather is really nice today.
The food is really delicious.
Oh, it is already this late.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 네요, like saying 좋아네요 instead of the correct 좋네요.
Forgetting to drop ㄹ in ㄹ-stems, like saying 멀네요 instead of 머네요.
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 네요 directly with no vowel change
Drop ㄹ first if the stem ends in ㄹ
Use 았/었네요 for a reaction about the past
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: A/V-네요 is the little ending Koreans use to show they just noticed something, similar to saying oh or wow in English. You attach 네요 straight onto the stem with no vowel harmony, so 좋다 becomes 좋네요 (oh, it is nice) and 맛있다 becomes 맛있네요 (wow, it is tasty). It carries a soft, friendly feeling of fresh discovery, which is why it is so common in everyday conversation when you react to food, weather, or someone skill. Two things trip up beginners: do not insert 아/어 before 네요, and remember that ㄹ-stems lose the ㄹ, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, not 멀네요.

endingItems.title: Seeking Agreement
endingItems.plainEnglish: Asks the listener to confirm or agree with something you already believe is true.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you expect the listener to agree, like English right? or isn't it?, e.g. 오늘 날씨가 춥지요? (It is cold today, right?).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 지요 directly to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel harmony (춥다→춥지요, 가다→가지요, 좋다→좋지요). It commonly contracts to 죠 in speech (춥죠?). For past confirmation use 았/었지요 (갔지요?, 먹었지요?). With nouns use 이지요/지요 (학생이지요?).
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with a plain yes-no question A/V-아/어요?, which genuinely asks for unknown information, while A/V-지요? assumes a shared answer and just seeks agreement.

examples.en: The weather is really cold today, isn't it?
This movie is fun, right?
You like Korean food, right?
We are meeting tomorrow, right?

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 지요, like saying 좋아지요 instead of the correct 좋지요.
Using 지요? for truly unknown information when a plain question with 아/어요? is what you really need.
studyOrder: Find the plain stem by dropping 다
Attach 지요 with no vowel change
Contract to 죠 in casual speech
Use 았/었지요 to confirm a past fact
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: A/V-지요? is how Korean says right? or isn't it?, and you use it when you are fairly sure of the answer and just want the listener to agree. Attach 지요 straight onto the stem with no vowel harmony, so 춥다 becomes 춥지요? (it is cold, right?) and 가다 becomes 가지요?; in everyday speech this almost always shrinks to 죠, as in 춥죠?. The key intuition is that it assumes shared knowledge, so it feels warm and inclusive rather than truly questioning. The main pitfall is using it for information you genuinely do not know; for a real question, use a plain 아/어요? instead.

endingItems.title: Subject Honorific
endingItems.plainEnglish: Raises and respects the person who is doing the action, usually someone older or senior.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when the subject of the sentence deserves respect, like a teacher or grandparent, e.g. 선생님이 가세요 (The teacher is going).
endingItems.attachmentRule: After a vowel-ending stem add 시 (가다→가시다→가세요); after a consonant-ending stem add 으시 (받다→받으시다→받으세요). ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ then add 시 (살다→사시다→사세요). Some verbs are suppletive and change the whole word: 먹다/마시다→드시다 (드세요), 자다→주무시다, 있다→계시다, 말하다→말씀하시다.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with the plain non-honorific form: 가요 simply says someone goes, while 가세요 respectfully says an honored person goes.

examples.en: The teacher is coming now.
Grandfather is eating his meal.
Mother is at home.
The boss is reading the newspaper.

commonMistakes: Using the plain verb 먹어요 for a respected person instead of the suppletive honorific 드세요.
Forgetting 으 after a consonant stem, like saying 받세요 instead of the correct 받으세요.
studyOrder: Decide if the subject deserves respect
Add 시 after a vowel or 으시 after a consonant
Replace suppletive verbs like 먹다 with 드시다
Combine into the polite form, for example 가세요
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The honorific infix -(으)시- is how Korean shows respect to the person performing the action, which is essential when you talk about elders, teachers, or customers. After a vowel stem you add 시 and after a consonant stem you add 으시, so 가다 becomes 가세요 and 받다 becomes 받으세요 in the polite present. A few high-frequency verbs do not just add 시 but swap entirely: 먹다 and 마시다 become 드시다 (드세요), 있다 becomes 계시다, and 자다 becomes 주무시다, so these must be memorized. The biggest beginner pitfall is using a plain verb like 먹어요 about a respected person; with elders you should say 드세요 instead.

endingItems.title: Past Experience
endingItems.plainEnglish: Says whether you have or have not ever done something before.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to talk about life experiences, like English have you ever, e.g. 한국에 가 본 적 있어요? (Have you ever been to Korea?).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Make the past modifier on the stem: after a vowel-ending stem add ㄴ 적 (가다→간 적), after a consonant-ending stem add 은 적 (먹다→먹은 적). Then add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for have never done. ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ then add ㄴ (살다→산 적); ㄷ irregular 듣다→들은 적; it often pairs with 아/어 보다 as V-아/어 본 적 있다.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with the plain past V-았/었어요, which reports one specific finished event, while V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다 asks generally whether the experience has ever happened in your life.

examples.ko: 저는 한국에 가 본 적 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hanguge ga bon jeok isseoyo.
examples.en: I have been to Korea before.
I have never worn a hanbok.
I have heard that song before.
Have you ever made kimchi stew?

commonMistakes: Using the present modifier instead of the past one, like saying 가는 적 있어요 instead of the correct 간 적 있어요.
Forgetting 은 after a consonant stem, like saying 먹ㄴ 적 instead of 먹은 적.
studyOrder: Find the stem by dropping 다
Add ㄴ 적 after a vowel or 은 적 after a consonant
Add 있어요 for have done or 없어요 for never
Optionally combine with 아/어 본 적 있다
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 적 있다/없다 is the Korean way to talk about whether an experience has ever happened in your life, much like English have you ever. You first build the past modifier on the verb, adding ㄴ 적 after a vowel stem and 은 적 after a consonant stem, so 가다 becomes 간 적 and 먹다 becomes 먹은 적. Then 있어요 means you have done it and 없어요 means you never have, as in 한복을 입은 적 없어요 (I have never worn a hanbok). It very often teams up with 아/어 보다 to give V-아/어 본 적 있다, a soft natural way to ask about experience. The main pitfall is using the present modifier 가는 적 instead of the required past modifier 간 적.

endingItems.title: Comparison: more than
endingItems.plainEnglish: It marks the thing you are comparing against, like saying than in English.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to compare two things, often with 더 (more). Example: 기차가 버스보다 더 빨라요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 보다 directly to a noun with no spacing change, after both vowels and consonants (사과보다, 물보다). The pattern is A가/는 B보다 더 Adjective.
endingItems.contrastWith: 보다 marks the standard you compare to, while 처럼 means like or as (similar to), not more or less.

examples.en: My younger sibling is taller than me.
Today is colder than yesterday.
The train is faster than the bus.

examples.ko: 이 책이 저 책보다 더 재미있어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegi jeo chaekboda deo jaemiisseoyo.
examples.en: This book is more interesting than that book.

commonMistakes: Putting 보다 on the wrong noun; it attaches to the standard B, not to the subject A.
Translating 더 as required everywhere; 더 is common but optional and means more.
studyOrder: Identify the two items A and B you compare
Attach 보다 to the standard B
Add 더 before the adjective for more
Finish with the adjective in 해요 form
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 보다 is how Korean says than in a comparison, and it attaches to the thing you measure against, not to the subject. Think A가 B보다 더 (adjective): in 동생이 저보다 키가 더 커요, 저 (me) is the standard, so my sibling comes out taller. In 오늘이 어제보다 더 추워요, yesterday is the standard and today is colder. The word 더 means more and usually sits right before the adjective, though you can drop it and the sentence still compares. The most common pitfall is sticking 보다 onto the subject by mistake; remember it always glues to the item you are comparing to, which in English follows the word than.

endingItems.title: Optional plural marker
endingItems.plainEnglish: It marks a noun as plural, but Korean usually leaves it off.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to stress that there are many people or things, mostly with people. Example: 학생들이 교실에 있어요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 들 to the end of the noun after both vowels and consonants (친구들, 학생들). With a number or counter you normally omit it (사과 세 개, not 사과들 세 개).
endingItems.contrastWith: Unlike English -s, 들 is optional; a bare noun like 사과 can already mean apple or apples from context.

examples.en: The students are in the classroom.
I watch a movie together with my friends.
The children play in the park.
There are really many people.

commonMistakes: Adding 들 to every plural the way English uses -s; it is usually omitted and sounds heavy if overused.
Using 들 together with a number, like 사과들 세 개; drop 들 when a counter is present.
studyOrder: Notice Korean nouns do not need a plural mark
Add 들 only to highlight many, usually people
Attach 들 to the end of the noun
Drop 들 when a number or counter appears
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 들 turns a noun plural, but the key idea for beginners is that it is optional and Korean usually drops it. A bare noun like 사과 can mean apple or apples, and context tells you which, so you do not need 들 the way English forces -s. You see it most with people: 학생들이 교실에 있어요 (the students are in the classroom) or 친구들과 같이 가요 (I go with my friends). The main pitfall is sprinkling 들 onto everything; it sounds heavy, and you should especially leave it off when a counter is present, so say 사과 세 개 (three apples), never 사과들 세 개.

endingItems.title: Counting with counters
endingItems.plainEnglish: To count things you use a native number plus a counter word that matches the kind of thing.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it whenever you count objects, people, or animals. Example: 사과 두 개 주세요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Use NATIVE numbers before counters, and the numbers 1 to 4 change shape: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 (한 개, 두 명, 세 마리). Order is noun + number + counter (사과 세 개).
endingItems.contrastWith: Counters use native numbers (한, 두, 세), while dates, money, and minutes use Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼), so do not mix them.

examples.en: Two cups of coffee, please.
There are three students in the classroom.
I raise one puppy.
Two bottles of beer, please.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers with counters, like 이 개 instead of 두 개.
Forgetting that 1 to 4 change shape, saying 하나 개 instead of 한 개.
studyOrder: Pick the right counter: 개 things, 명 people, 마리 animals, 잔 cups, 병 bottles
Choose a native number
Change 1 to 4 to 한, 두, 세, 네 before the counter
Say it as noun + number + counter
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean cannot count things with a number alone; you need a counter word that matches the category, and you use native numbers in front of it. The everyday counters are 개 for objects, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups or glasses, and 병 for bottles, so you say 사과 두 개 (two apples) and 학생 세 명 (three students). The big rule to memorize is that the native numbers one through four shorten before a counter: 하나 둘 셋 넷 become 한 두 세 네, giving 한 개, 두 명, 세 마리. The classic pitfall is reaching for Sino numbers like 이 or 삼; those are for dates and money, so counting people as 이 명 is wrong and you want 두 명 instead.

endingItems.title: Background or soft contrast
endingItems.plainEnglish: It sets up background information or a gentle but before the next clause.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to give a situation, then add a reaction, request, or contrast. Example: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: For verbs and 있다/없다 add -는데 to the stem (가는데, 먹는데). For adjectives add -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). Past tense uses -았/었는데 (갔는데).
endingItems.contrastWith: -지만 is a plain but for direct contrast, while -는데 is softer and also sets a scene or lead-in, not only contrast.

examples.en: It is raining but I do not have an umbrella.
This restaurant is tasty but a bit expensive.
I am studying now and it is very hard.
It is the weekend, so shall we watch a movie together?

commonMistakes: Using verb ending -은데 for verbs; verbs take -는데 (먹는데), and -은데 is for adjectives.
Treating -는데 as a strong but; it is softer and often just sets background for what follows.

practiceItems.prompt: it is the weekend, so (shall we watch a movie)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
For verbs and 있다/없다 use -는데
For adjectives use -은데 or -ㄴ데
Add the reaction, request, or contrast in the next clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -는데 is a soft connector that paints the background first and then lets you add a reaction, a question, a request, or a light contrast. Picture giving the scene, then the point: 비가 오는데 우산이 없어요 (it is raining, and I have no umbrella) or 주말인데 같이 영화 볼래요? (it is the weekend, so shall we see a movie?). The attachment depends on word type: verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데 (가는데, 먹는데), while adjectives take -은데 after a consonant and -ㄴ데 after a vowel (작은데, 큰데). The main pitfall is mixing these up and saying 먹은데 for a verb; verbs always use -는데, and remember this ending is gentler than the blunt 지만.

endingItems.title: Doing two things at once
endingItems.plainEnglish: It links two actions that one person does at the same time.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when the same subject does two actions simultaneously. Example: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -으면서 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹으면서, 읽으면서) and -면서 to a stem ending in a vowel (가면서, 보면서). The subject of both actions must be the same person.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)면서 means doing two things at once, while -고 just lists or sequences actions that need not overlap in time.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
I watch television while eating.
We talk while drinking coffee.
I clean while singing a song.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)면서 for two different subjects; both actions must share one subject.
Forgetting -으- after a consonant stem, saying 먹면서 instead of 먹으면서.
studyOrder: Check that one subject does both actions
Find the verb stem
Add -면서 after a vowel or -으면서 after a consonant
Put the simultaneous action in the second clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -(으)면서 joins two actions that one person performs at the very same time, like our word while. The rule is one subject doing both: 음악을 들으면서 공부해요 means I study while listening to music, and 밥을 먹으면서 텔레비전을 봐요 means I watch TV while eating. Attachment follows the usual vowel and consonant split: vowel-final stems take -면서 (가면서, 보면서) and consonant-final stems take -으면서 (먹으면서, 읽으면서). Two pitfalls trip up beginners: do not use it when the two clauses have different subjects, and do not drop the linking 으 after a consonant, so it is 먹으면서, never 먹면서. Compare it with -고, which only lists actions and does not force them to overlap.

endingItems.title: Before doing something
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you do the main action before another action happens.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to say before doing a verb. Example: 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -기 전에 to any verb stem with no vowel or consonant change (먹기 전에, 가기 전에, 자기 전에). For before a noun, use Noun 전에 instead (식사 전에).
endingItems.contrastWith: -기 전에 means before doing, while its opposite -(으)ㄴ 후에 means after doing; pick by which action comes first.

examples.en: I wash my hands before I eat.
I read a book before I sleep.
I turn off the light before leaving home.
I drink water before exercising.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 전에, like 먹어기 전에; always use the plain stem plus -기 전에 (먹기 전에).
Using -기 전에 with a noun; for nouns use Noun 전에, for example 식사 전에, not 식사기 전에.

practiceItems.prompt: before going out (I turn off the light)

studyOrder: Find the action that happens later, the main verb
Take its plain dictionary stem
Add -기 전에 with no spelling change
Place the earlier event in the main clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-기 전에 lets you say you do something before another action takes place, and it is wonderfully regular because you just add -기 전에 to the plain verb stem with no changes. Look at 밥을 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요 (I wash my hands before I eat) and 자기 전에 책을 읽어요 (I read before I sleep): the verb after 전에 is the later event, and the main clause tells what you do first. For nouns you switch to Noun 전에, as in 식사 전에 (before the meal), not 식사기 전에. The number one pitfall is conjugating the verb, writing 먹어기 전에; keep it as the bare stem 먹기. Remember its mirror image -(으)ㄴ 후에 for after, and choose based on which action comes first.

endingItems.title: After doing something
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you do the main action after another action is finished.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to say after doing a verb. Example: 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Add -은 후에 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and -ㄴ 후에 to a stem ending in a vowel (간 후에, 본 후에). For after a noun, use Noun 후에 (식사 후에). You can replace 후에 with 다음에 or 뒤에.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄴ 후에 means after doing and uses a past-style -은/-ㄴ form, while -기 전에 means before doing and keeps the plain stem.

examples.en: I drink coffee after I eat.
I go home after class ends.
I eat after I wash my hands.
I shower after exercising.

commonMistakes: Using the plain stem like -기, saying 먹기 후에; after needs the -은/-ㄴ form, so 먹은 후에.
Forgetting the consonant and vowel split, writing 간 후에 as 가은 후에; vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에).
studyOrder: Find the action that happens first
Add -은 후에 after a consonant or -ㄴ 후에 after a vowel
Put the later action in the main clause
Swap 후에 for 다음에 or 뒤에 if you like
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 후에 expresses that you do the main action after another one is finished, and it pairs as the opposite of -기 전에. Unlike before, the after pattern uses the -은/-ㄴ ending: consonant stems take -은 후에 (먹은 후에, 읽은 후에) and vowel stems take -ㄴ 후에 (간 후에, 본 후에). So 밥을 먹은 후에 커피를 마셔요 means I drink coffee after eating, and 수업이 끝난 후에 집에 가요 means I go home after class ends; the verb before 후에 is the earlier event. For nouns use Noun 후에, like 식사 후에, and you may freely replace 후에 with 다음에 or 뒤에. The main pitfall is reusing the plain -기 stem from the before pattern; for after you must say 먹은 후에, not 먹기 후에.

endingItems.title: Every or each
endingItems.plainEnglish: It attaches to a noun to mean every or each one.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for repeated times or each member of a group. Example: 주말마다 운동해요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach 마다 directly to the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change (아침마다, 주말마다, 사람마다). With time words it means every; with people or things it means each.
endingItems.contrastWith: 마다 means every or each, while 매- as in 매일 or 매주 is a fixed prefix on set time words; 마다 attaches freely to many nouns.

examples.en: I exercise every weekend.
I drink coffee every morning.
Each person thinks differently.
I study Korean every day.

commonMistakes: Adding a particle after 마다 when none is needed, like 주말마다에; 마다 already carries the meaning.
Confusing 마다 with 매-; 매일 is fixed, but 마다 attaches freely, as in 주말마다.
studyOrder: Pick the noun you want to repeat or distribute
Attach 마다 directly with no spelling change
Read it as every for time words
Read it as each for people or things
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: N마다 attaches to a noun and means every or each, covering both repeated times and every member of a group. With time words it lands on every: 주말마다 운동해요 (I exercise every weekend) and 아침마다 커피를 마셔요 (I drink coffee every morning). With people or things it shades toward each: 사람마다 생각이 달라요 means each person thinks differently. Attachment could not be simpler, since 마다 glues straight onto the noun after both vowels and consonants with no change. Two pitfalls: do not pile another particle on top, so avoid 주말마다에, because 마다 already does the job; and do not confuse it with the prefix 매-, which only sits on fixed words like 매일 or 매주, whereas 마다 attaches freely to almost any noun.

endingItems.title: Casual speech (banmal)
endingItems.plainEnglish: The informal style you use with close friends, people younger than you, and your partner, made by dropping the polite -요 / -습니다 endings.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it once you and the other person have agreed to drop formalities, with people clearly younger than you, with close same-age friends, with your boyfriend/girlfriend, and with little kids. A friend might say '우리 말 놓을까?' (should we drop the formal speech?) before you switch. Example: 폰 봤어? 답장 왜 안 해? (Did you see your phone? Why didn't you reply?)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the polite present form and remove -요: 먹어요 → 먹어, 가요 → 가, 좋아요 → 좋아. For nouns, 학생이에요 → 학생이야 (after a consonant) / 친구예요 → 친구야 (after a vowel). Questions, statements, and suggestions all use the same -아/어 form with intonation doing the work: 갈래? / 갈래 / 같이 가. Commands drop -요 too (가 / 먹어), and 'let's' uses -자 (가자, 먹자). Past stays -았/었어 (먹었어), future -ㄹ 거야 (갈 거야).
endingItems.contrastWith: 반말 vs 존댓말 (요/습니다 polite speech): same verb, different ending. 어디 가요? is polite, 어디 가? is casual. Using 반말 with a stranger, an older person you just met, or a boss sounds rude or like you're picking a fight, so default to 존댓말 until you've clearly agreed to switch.

examples.en: Hey, what time are we meeting today?
I'm on my way, just wait five minutes.

examples.ko: 우리 이제 말 편하게 하자, 동갑이잖아.
examples.romanization: uri ije mal pyeonhage haja, donggabijana.
examples.en: Let's talk casually from now on, we're the same age.
Isn't that so funny? lol

commonMistakes: Switching to 반말 with someone older or a stranger before they offer — it comes off as disrespectful, so wait until they say it's okay.
Keeping -요 stuck on by habit (가요? to a close friend) — drop it fully, and remember the noun ending becomes -야/-이야, not -예요.

practiceItems.prompt: Make '내일 시간 있어요?' casual (to a close friend)

studyOrder: First learn the polite -요 forms, since 반말 is just those with -요 removed.
Practice the noun endings -야 / -이야 and the 'let's' ending -자 separately.
Listen to how friends signal the switch ('말 놓자', '편하게 해') so you know when it's socially safe to use.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: 반말 is the relaxed way Koreans talk to people they're close to or younger than. The trick is simple: take the polite sentence and chop off the -요 at the end. 좋아요 becomes 좋아, 어디 가요? becomes 어디 가? Be careful, though — Korean cares a lot about who you're talking to, so you only use 반말 with friends, your partner, kids, or after an older person tells you it's fine. With strangers and elders, stay polite. When in doubt, keep the -요 and listen for the moment someone says '편하게 말해' (talk casually) — that's your green light.

endingItems.title: -jana: 'you know / as you know'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to remind someone of something you both already know, or to gently point out a reason they should have realized.
endingItems.whenToUse: When the listener already knows (or should know) the fact and you're nudging them with it. Great for explaining why you can't do something or correcting a wrong assumption softly. Example: 나 오늘 못 가, 내일 시험 있잖아. (I can't go today — I have an exam tomorrow, remember?)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -잖아 directly to the verb/adjective stem; add -요 to be polite. Present: 있다 → 있잖아(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘잖아(요). Past: use -았/었잖아 (갔잖아, 먹었잖아). For nouns: -(이)잖아 → 학생이잖아 (after consonant) / 친구잖아 (after vowel). No irregular sound changes beyond the normal stem.
endingItems.contrastWith: -잖아 vs -거든(요): -잖아 means 'as you ALREADY know' (shared info), while -거든 introduces info that's NEW to the listener. 'I can't, I'm busy 바쁘잖아' = you knew I was busy; '바쁘거든' = letting you know now (and can sound a bit blunt/defensive).

examples.ko: 왜 또 늦었어? 차 막히는 시간이잖아.
examples.romanization: wae tto neujeosseo? cha makineun siganijana.
examples.en: Why are you late again? It's rush hour, you know.

examples.ko: 그 카페 주말엔 사람 진짜 많잖아, 평일에 가자.
examples.romanization: geu kape jumaren saram jinjja manchana, pyeongire gaja.
examples.en: That cafe is super crowded on weekends, you know — let's go on a weekday.

examples.ko: 내가 매운 거 못 먹잖아, 딴 거 시키자.
examples.romanization: naega maeun geo mon meokjana, ttan geo sikija.
examples.en: You know I can't eat spicy food — let's order something else.
I told you yesterday, remember — there's a work dinner today.

commonMistakes: Using -잖아 with a brand-new fact the listener couldn't know — it sounds like you're blaming them for not knowing. Use -거든(요) or plain statements instead.
Using -잖아 with a senior/stranger; even with -요 it can feel like 'you should already know this,' so it's mainly for friends and familiar people.

practiceItems.prompt: Remind a friend: 'It's payday today, you know' (월급날)
Politely remind a coworker: 'That meeting is tomorrow, you know' (회의)

studyOrder: Learn it first as 'remember?' — a reminder of shared knowledge.
Practice the past form -았/었잖아 since you'll often remind people of past events.
Contrast it side by side with -거든 so you don't mix up 'you know already' vs 'just so you know'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -잖아(요) is the 'you know' / 'remember?' ending. You stick it on when you're reminding the other person of something they already know, like 'It's rush hour, you know' or 'I can't eat spicy food, remember?' It makes your reason feel shared rather than like new information. Add -요 to keep it polite (있잖아요), or drop it with friends (있잖아). One caution: don't use it for facts the listener has no way of knowing — that comes across as 'why didn't you know this?' Save -잖아 for stuff you've both got in your heads already.

endingItems.title: -geodeun: 'just so you know / it's because'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to give a reason or piece of background info that the listener doesn't know yet, often as a comeback or explanation.
endingItems.whenToUse: When you're telling someone something new — explaining why, or setting up more to come. Example: 나 오늘 일찍 가야 돼. 부모님 오시거든. (I have to leave early today — my parents are coming over, you see.) In texts it often answers a 'why?' with a touch of attitude: 그냥 좀 바쁘거든.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -거든 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present: 가다 → 가거든(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁘거든(요). Past: -았/었거든 (먹었거든, 갔거든). Future/plan: -(으)ㄹ 거거든 (갈 거거든). Nouns: -(이)거든(요) → 학생이거든요 / 친구거든요. Sentence-final intonation falls; it commonly sets up a follow-up sentence.
endingItems.contrastWith: -거든 vs -잖아: -거든 gives NEW info ('just so you know'), -잖아 recalls SHARED info ('as you know'). Also vs -아서/-니까 (reason): those connect inside one sentence (바빠서 못 가), while -거든 ends the sentence and adds a 'here's the backstory' feel. Standalone -거든(요) can sound mildly sassy/defensive, so tone matters.
sentenceFrames: 사실 나 ___ 거든 (Actually, I ___, you see)

examples.ko: 나 그 드라마 벌써 다 봤거든, 스포 하지 마.
examples.romanization: na geu deurama beolsseo da bwatgeodeun, seupo haji ma.
examples.en: I've already finished that drama, you see, so no spoilers.

examples.ko: 오늘은 좀 일찍 들어가야 돼. 내일 출근해야 하거든.
examples.romanization: oneureun jom iljjik deureogaya dwae. naeil chulgeunhaeya hageodeun.
examples.en: I have to head home early today — I've got work tomorrow, you see.

examples.ko: 사실 나 그 사람이랑 아는 사이거든. 소개해 줄까?
examples.romanization: sasil na geu saramirang aneun saigeodeun. sogaehae julkka?
examples.en: Actually I know that person — want me to introduce you?

examples.ko: 왜 화났냐고? 네가 약속 또 깼거든.
examples.romanization: wae hwanannyago? nega yaksok tto kkaetgeodeun.
examples.en: Why am I mad? Because you broke your promise again, that's why.

commonMistakes: Using -거든 for info the listener already knows — that's -잖아's job; -거든 should feel like fresh news.
Overusing standalone -거든요 with seniors: the slightly defensive tone can read as 'well, FYI…', so soften with a full reason in formal settings.

practiceItems.prompt: Explain (new info): 'I have to leave early, I have plans' (약속 있다)
practiceItems.ko: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.
practiceItems.answer: 나 일찍 가야 돼, 약속 있거든.

practiceItems.prompt: Tell a friend (new info): 'I already ate' (먹다)
Politely explain to a coworker: 'I'm a bit busy right now, you see' (바쁘다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'just so you know / here's why' — info the listener didn't have.
Practice using it to set up a second sentence (reason → then what you'll do).
Compare it directly with -잖아 (new vs shared info) to lock in the difference.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -거든(요) is how you drop new background info on someone — 'just so you know.' If a friend asks why you're leaving early, you say 내일 일찍 출근하거든 (because I have early work tomorrow, you see). It often leads into a second sentence that explains what happens next. Think of -잖아 and -거든 as a pair: -잖아 is 'as you already know,' -거든 is 'something you didn't know.' Add -요 to be polite. Heads up: said all by itself with a sharp tone, -거든요 can sound a little sassy ('well, FYI'), so among friends it's playful, but with elders soften it with a full explanation.

endingItems.title: -deorago: 'I noticed / turns out'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to report something you personally saw, felt, or discovered in the past — sharing a firsthand impression.
endingItems.whenToUse: When you're recounting something you directly experienced and it struck you. Perfect for reviews and gossip. Example: 그 집 가 봤는데 생각보다 비싸더라고. (I went to that place and it was pricier than I expected, turns out.) Used a ton when telling friends about food, people, or places you tried.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -더라고 to the plain stem; add -요 for politeness. Present-experience: 비싸다 → 비싸더라고(요), 있다 → 있더라고(요). Past (already happened before you noticed): -았/었더라고 (갔더라고요 = turns out they had gone). Nouns: -(이)더라고(요) → 진짜 맛집이더라고요. Key restriction: for your OWN direct observation. With first-person feelings, only inner states work (나 그때 진짜 떨리더라고 = I was so nervous then).
endingItems.contrastWith: -더라고 vs plain past -았/었어: plain past just states a fact (비쌌어 = it was expensive). -더라고 adds 'and I noticed it myself / it stood out to me,' giving an eyewitness, slightly surprised flavor. Also vs -대(요) (hearsay): -더라고 = I saw it; -대 = I heard it from someone.
sentenceFrames: 가 보니까 ___ 더라고 (When I went, it was ___, turns out)
그 사람 ___ 더라고요 (That person was ___, I noticed)
막상 해 보니까 ___ 더라고 (Once I actually tried it, it was ___)

examples.ko: 거기 분위기 진짜 좋더라고, 데이트하기 딱이야.
examples.romanization: geogi bunwigi jinjja joteorago, deiteuhagi ttagiya.
examples.en: The vibe there was really nice, turns out — perfect for a date.
I ordered on Baemin and it came faster than I expected, actually.
The new team lead is really meticulous, I noticed.

examples.ko: 월세가 생각보다 너무 비싸더라고, 그래서 좀 더 외곽으로 알아봤어.
examples.romanization: wolsega saenggakboda neomu bissadeorago, geuraeseo jom deo oegwageuro arabwasseo.
examples.en: The rent was way pricier than I thought, so I looked a bit further out.

commonMistakes: Using -더라고 for things you only heard about — if you didn't witness it yourself, use -대(요) (hearsay) instead.
Saying 나 똑똑하더라고 (I'm smart, I noticed) — you can't 'observe' your own permanent traits this way; -더라고 with 'I' works only for inner feelings/states you experienced (떨리더라고, 좋더라고).

practiceItems.prompt: Report from a visit: 'The food there was really good, turns out' (맛있다)
Tell a coworker you noticed: 'The new cafe is always crowded' (사람 많다)
practiceItems.ko: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.
practiceItems.answer: 새로 생긴 카페 항상 사람 많더라고요.

practiceItems.prompt: Share your feeling: 'I was really nervous then' (떨리다)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I saw/felt it firsthand, and here's my take.'
Practice pairing it with 가 보니까 / 해 보니까 (when I went/tried) to frame the experience.
Compare -더라고 (I witnessed) with -대 (I heard) so you report sources correctly.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -더라고(요) is your 'firsthand report' ending. When you've personally seen, tried, or felt something, you use it to tell others your impression: 거기 진짜 좋더라고 (turns out that place is really nice). It carries a little 'I noticed this myself, and it kind of surprised me' feeling, which is why Koreans use it constantly for reviewing restaurants, cafes, and people. Add -요 to be polite. Two rules to remember: only use it for things YOU witnessed (for stuff you just heard, use -대), and don't use it to describe your own personality — only your own feelings, like 떨리더라고 (I was nervous).

endingItems.title: -na boda: 'I guess / it seems'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to make a guess based on some evidence you're seeing or hearing right now — 'it looks like / I guess so.'
endingItems.whenToUse: When you infer something from a clue, not direct knowledge. Example: 답장 없는 거 보니까 바쁜가 봐. (Going by the no-reply, I guess they're busy.) Super common for guessing about other people's situations and feelings without being pushy.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Verbs (action): stem + -나 보다 → 오다 → 오나 보다, 먹다 → 먹나 보다 (past: 먹었나 보다). Adjectives & 이다 (state): stem + -(으)ㄴ가 보다 → 좋다 → 좋은가 보다, 바쁘다 → 바쁜가 보다, 학생이다 → 학생인가 보다. In speech people very often just say -나 봐 for both (좋나 봐 is widely used colloquially). Conjugate 보다 normally: 봐(요), 봐서, 봤어.
endingItems.contrastWith: -나 보다 vs -것 같다: both mean 'seems,' but -나 보다 is an inference from outside evidence about OTHER people/situations (그 집 잘되나 봐 = looks like that shop's doing well, judging by the crowd). -것 같다 is a broader, softer personal opinion that can also be about yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아). You normally don't use -나 보다 about your own clear feelings.
sentenceFrames: ___ 나 봐 (I guess they ___ / it seems they ___)

examples.en: They read it and didn't reply — I guess they're busy.

examples.ko: 사람들이 줄 선 거 보니까 거기 맛집인가 봐.
examples.romanization: saramdeuri jul seon geo bonikka geogi matjibinga bwa.
examples.en: Going by the line, I guess that place is really good.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 표정 보니까 일 때문에 스트레스 많이 받나 봐.
examples.romanization: gyae yojeum pyojeong bonikka il ttaemune seuteureseu mani banna bwa.
examples.en: From their face lately, I guess work is stressing them out a lot.

examples.ko: 불 꺼져 있는 거 보니까 다들 퇴근했나 봐요.
examples.romanization: bul kkeojyeo inneun geo bonikka dadeul toegeunhaenna bwayo.
examples.en: The lights are off, so I guess everyone's gone home.

commonMistakes: Choosing the wrong connector: verbs take -나 보다, adjectives/이다 take -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋나 보다 is colloquial but 좋은가 봐 is the textbook-correct form).
Using -나 보다 about your own obvious feelings (나 배고프나 봐 sounds odd) — you know your own state, so use -것 같다 or just state it.

practiceItems.prompt: Guess from evidence: 'I guess it's raining outside' (비 오다)
Infer about a coworker: 'I guess the new place is expensive' (비싸다)
Guess about a friend: 'I guess they already left' (가다, past)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I guess, based on a clue I can see/hear.'
Drill the verb (-나) vs adjective/이다 (-(으)ㄴ가) split with a few example pairs.
Compare with -것 같다 so you know when it's an evidence-based guess about others vs a general soft opinion.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -나 보다 is how you make an educated guess from a clue in front of you. You see a long line at a restaurant and say 맛집인가 봐 (I guess it's a good spot); someone isn't texting back and you say 바쁜가 봐 (I guess they're busy). It's mostly for guessing about other people or situations, not your own feelings — you already know how you feel. One small grammar point: action verbs use -나 보다 (오나 봐), while adjectives and 이다 use -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋은가 봐), though in fast speech you'll hear -나 봐 used loosely for everything. Just conjugate 보다 like a normal verb at the end: 봐, 봐요.

endingItems.title: -neunde: soft, open-ended ending
endingItems.plainEnglish: Ending a sentence on -는데(요) leaves it gently hanging, softening a reply, hinting at a 'but…', or inviting the other person to react.
endingItems.whenToUse: When you want to sound less blunt — answering, mild disagreement, leaving room for a response. Example: 지금은 좀 바쁜데요… (I'm a little busy right now… [so maybe later?]). Also for a surprised/impressed reaction: 오, 잘하는데? (Oh, you're pretty good!). Hugely useful for polite refusals and soft pushback at work.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Verbs & 있다/없다: stem + -는데(요) → 가다 → 가는데(요), 먹다 → 먹는데(요), 있다 → 있는데(요). Adjectives & 이다: stem + -(으)ㄴ데(요) → 좋다 → 좋은데(요), 바쁘다 → 바쁜데(요), 학생이다 → 학생인데(요). Past (all): -았/었는데(요) → 갔는데(요), 먹었는데(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -ㄴ데 (멀다 → 먼데요, 길다 → 긴데요). Trailing intonation rises or trails off to create the soft, open feel.
endingItems.contrastWith: Sentence-final -는데(요) (soft, trailing) vs connective -는데 (mid-sentence 'but/and' that links two clauses: 비싼데 맛있어 = it's pricey but tasty). Same form, but the ending version stops there to leave things open. Vs flat -아/어요: 바빠요 is a hard 'I'm busy'; 바쁜데요… softens it into 'I'm kind of busy (so…)', much friendlier for declining.
sentenceFrames: 지금은 좀 ___ 는데요… (It's a bit ___ right now, so…)
어, 생각보다 ___ 는데? (Oh, that's more ___ than I expected!)

examples.ko: 그 날은 제가 선약이 있는데요, 다른 날은 어때요?
examples.romanization: geu nareun jega seonyagi inneundeyo, dareun nareun eottaeyo?
examples.en: I have other plans that day… how about another day?
Huh? You're actually really good at singing!
Hmm… that price is a little much for me, though.

examples.ko: 저는 이미 다 끝냈는데요? 안 받으셨어요?
examples.romanization: jeoneun imi da kkeunnaenneundeyo? an badeusyeosseoyo?
examples.en: I already finished it all, though? You didn't get it?

commonMistakes: Mixing up the verb (-는데) and adjective (-(으)ㄴ데) forms: 좋는데 is wrong → 좋은데(요); 바쁘는데 is wrong → 바쁜데(요).
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 멀는데요 is wrong → 먼데요; 길는데요 → 긴데요.

practiceItems.prompt: Softly decline: 'I'm a little busy right now…' (바쁘다)
React, impressed: 'Oh, this is pretty tasty!' (맛있다)
Soft pushback: 'I already sent it, though' (보내다, past)

studyOrder: Learn the soft 'trailing off' feel first — it's the politeness superpower of casual Korean.
Drill verb -는데 vs adjective -(으)ㄴ데 and the ㄹ-drop with a few pairs.
Then notice the connective use mid-sentence ('but/and') so you recognize both jobs of the same form.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -는데(요) is one of the most useful endings for sounding natural and polite. Instead of giving a hard, flat answer, you let the sentence trail off, which feels softer and invites the other person to respond. 'I'm busy' as 바빠요 sounds final, but 바쁜데요… feels like 'I'm kind of busy, so maybe we figure something out.' It's also a great reaction when you're pleasantly surprised: 잘하는데? (oh, you're good!). Watch the form: action verbs and 있다/없다 take -는데, while adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ데, and ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ (멀다 → 먼데요). The same shape also works mid-sentence as a gentle 'but,' so you'll see it everywhere.

endingItems.title: -eulge: 'I'll (do it), promise'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to announce what YOU will do, usually as a promise or a response to the listener — 'I'll do it / I'll take care of it.'
endingItems.whenToUse: First person only, reacting to the situation or the other person. Example: 나 먼저 갈게, 이따 연락해. (I'll head out first — text me later.) All over KakaoTalk: 곧 갈게요, 확인하고 답장할게요. Shows you're committing to the action for the listener's benefit.
endingItems.attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ게(요) → 가다 → 갈게(요), 만들다 → 만들게(요) (ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ, no doubling). After other consonants: -을게(요) → 먹다 → 먹을게(요), 읽다 → 읽을게(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을게(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울게(요). Pronounced [ㄹ께]. First person subject only; no past form.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ게(요) vs -(으)ㄹ래(요): -ㄹ게 is a one-sided promise/decision made FOR or in response to the listener (내가 살게 = I'll pay). -ㄹ래 expresses your own preference or asks the other's (나 집에 갈래 = I want to go home / 갈래? = wanna go?). Also vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (plain future plan): 갈 거예요 just states a plan; 갈게요 feels like a promise responding to you.
sentenceFrames: 먼저 ___ 고 있을게 (I'll be ___ ahead of you)

examples.ko: 이번 커피는 내가 살게, 너 지난번에 샀잖아.
examples.romanization: ibeon keopineun naega salge, neo jinanbeone satjana.
examples.en: I'll get the coffee this time — you paid last time.
I'll text you on KakaoTalk when I get home!

examples.ko: 그 자료 제가 오늘 안에 정리해서 보낼게요.
examples.romanization: geu jaryo jega oneul ane jeongnihaeseo bonaelgeyo.
examples.en: I'll organize that file and send it by end of day.
I'll go in and wait — take your time.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ게요 with a third person (그 사람이 갈게요 is wrong) — it's strictly 'I/we will.' For others, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
Spelling it -ㄹ께요 in writing — the standard spelling is -ㄹ게요 even though it sounds like [께].

practiceItems.prompt: Promise a friend: 'I'll text you when I arrive' (연락하다)
Tell your boss: 'I'll finish it by today' (끝내다)
Offer: 'I'll listen' / 'I'll hear you out' (듣다, ㄷ-irregular)

studyOrder: Learn it as 'I'll do it (for you / in response to you)' — a promise, first person only.
Drill the consonant split (-ㄹ게 vs -을게) and the 듣다→들을게, 돕다→도울게 irregulars.
Contrast with -ㄹ래 (preference) and -ㄹ 거예요 (neutral plan) so the nuance is clear.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ게(요) is how you tell someone what you'll do, like a little promise. You text a friend 도착하면 연락할게 (I'll contact you when I arrive) or tell your boss 오늘 끝낼게요 (I'll finish today). The key feeling is that you're committing to the action partly for the listener — it's responsive, not just a cold statement of plans. Only use it about yourself (or 'we'); for what someone else will do, switch to -(으)ㄹ 거예요. Attach -ㄹ게 after a vowel (갈게) and -을게 after a consonant (먹을게), and note it's pronounced like '께' but you write it 게.

endingItems.title: -eullae: 'wanna…? / I think I'll…'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to ask what the other person feels like doing, or to state your own preference/intention casually — 'wanna…?' or 'I'm gonna…'.
endingItems.whenToUse: Inviting someone or voicing what you'd like. Example: 우리 영화 볼래? (Wanna watch a movie?) / 나 그냥 집에 있을래. (I think I'll just stay home.) The go-to for suggesting hangouts and dates in a relaxed way.
endingItems.attachmentRule: After a vowel or ㄹ: -ㄹ래(요) → 가다 → 갈래(요), 놀다 → 놀래(요). After other consonants: -을래(요) → 먹다 → 먹을래(요), 앉다 → 앉을래(요). ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들을래(요); ㅂ-irregular: 돕다 → 도울래(요). Question = rising intonation (갈래?), statement = falling (갈래). First/second person; not for stating a third person's wish.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ래(요) vs -(으)ㄹ까(요): -ㄹ래 asks the listener's preference or states yours (영화 볼래? = do you wanna watch?). -ㄹ까 proposes/wonders together (영화 볼까? = shall we watch?). -ㄹ까 feels more 'let's decide together / I'm wondering,' -ㄹ래 feels more 'what do YOU want?'. As a statement, 갈래 = personal will (a bit insistent if overused with elders), so keep it for friends.
sentenceFrames: 나 그냥 ___ 을래 (I think I'll just ___)
뭐 ___ ㄹ래요? (What would you like to ___?)

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 한강 갈래? 날씨 좋대.
examples.romanization: ibeon jumare hangang gallae? nalssi jotae.
examples.en: Wanna go to the Han River this weekend? They say the weather's nice.

examples.ko: 나 오늘 좀 피곤해서 그냥 집에서 쉴래.
examples.romanization: na oneul jom pigonhaeseo geunyang jibeseo swillae.
