examples.en: I'm kind of tired today, so I think I'll just rest at home.
Wanna grab coffee, or just head off?
What do you wanna eat? I'll treat.

commonMistakes: Using -(으)ㄹ래요? to invite a senior/boss — it can sound too casual or even pushy; use -(으)시겠어요? or -(으)ㄹ까요? instead.
Using it for a third person's desire (그 사람 갈래요 is wrong) — for that, use 가고 싶어 하다 (그 사람 가고 싶어 해).

practiceItems.prompt: State your preference: 'I think I'll just go home' (가다)
Ask casually: 'Wanna hang out this weekend?' (놀다, ㄹ-stem)

studyOrder: Learn it as the friendly 'wanna…?' for invitations and your own 'I think I'll…'.
Practice the consonant split and the 듣다→들을래, 돕다→도울래 irregulars.
Compare with -ㄹ까 ('shall we / I wonder') so you pick the right invitation nuance.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ래(요) is your everyday 'wanna…?' With friends you ask 영화 볼래? (wanna watch a movie?) or 뭐 먹을래? (what do you wanna eat?), and you state your own choice with 나 집에 있을래 (I think I'll stay home). Rising tone makes it a question, falling tone makes it a statement. It's relaxed and friendly, which is exactly why you should NOT aim it at a boss or someone much older — there it can sound too casual or even a little bossy, so use 같이 가실래요? carefully or switch to -ㄹ까요?. Attach -ㄹ래 after a vowel (갈래) and -을래 after a consonant (먹을래).

endingItems.title: -jyo: 'right? / isn't it?'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to confirm something you already believe is true and expect the listener to agree with — 'right? / you know how it is.'
endingItems.whenToUse: Seeking agreement or stating an obvious shared truth. Example: 오늘 진짜 덥죠? (It's really hot today, right?) Great small talk and for politely confirming plans: 내일 두 시 맞죠? (Tomorrow at two, right?). -죠 is just the contracted, very common spoken form of -지요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -지(요) / -죠 to the plain stem. Present: 덥다 → 덥지(요)/덥죠, 가다 → 가지(요)/가죠. Past: -았/었죠 → 갔죠, 먹었죠. Nouns: -(이)죠 → 맞죠, 친구죠. As a question (rising tone) it asks for agreement; as a statement (falling) it asserts 'of course/obviously.' Also softens commands/suggestions: 같이 가죠 (let's go, shall we), 그만하시죠 (let's stop).
endingItems.contrastWith: -죠? vs -잖아(요): -죠? asks the listener to CONFIRM/agree right now ('it's hot, right?'), while -잖아 reminds them of something already known ('it's summer, you know'). Vs plain -아요?: 더워요? is a genuine question (you don't know); 덥죠? assumes you both feel it and just want a nod.
sentenceFrames: 그건 당연히 ___ 죠 (That's obviously ___, of course)

examples.en: The dak-galbi here is really good, right?
Tomorrow's meetup is at seven, right?
Of course I should help you.
The weather's nice, so let's go grab a drink, shall we.

commonMistakes: Using -죠? when you genuinely don't know the answer — that's a real question, so use -아요?/-어요?. -죠? presumes the listener will agree.
Writing -죠 as -줘 — they're different; -죠 is the -지요 contraction (confirmation), 줘 is 'give (to me).'

practiceItems.prompt: Confirm with a coworker: 'The meeting's at 3, right?' (맞다)
Small talk: 'It's really cold today, right?' (춥다)

studyOrder: Learn -죠? as the tag question 'right?' that expects a yes.
Then learn the falling-tone statement use ('of course / obviously').
Contrast with -잖아 (reminder) and plain -아요? (real question) to place it precisely.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -지요, almost always shortened to -죠, is the 'right?' ending. You use it when you're pretty sure of something and just want the other person to agree: 오늘 덥죠? (it's hot today, right?) or 내일 두 시 맞죠? (tomorrow at two, right?). With a falling tone it instead means 'of course' — 당연히 제가 사죠 (of course I'll pay). It's friendly and great for small talk and confirming plans. Don't use it when you truly don't know the answer, though; if it's a real question, use -아요?/어요?. And don't confuse the spelling with 줘 (give) — -죠 comes from -지요.

endingItems.title: -neyo: realization / reaction
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to react to something you've just noticed, learned, or felt in the moment — surprise, admiration, or a fresh realization.
endingItems.whenToUse: On-the-spot reactions to new info or what's in front of you. Example: 와, 여기 진짜 예쁘네요! (Wow, this place is really pretty!) Perfect for reacting to photos, food, weather, or news a friend just told you. Adds a warm, spontaneous tone.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -네(요) to the plain stem. Present: 예쁘다 → 예쁘네(요), 많다 → 많네(요), 오다 → 오네(요). Past: -았/었네(요) → 벌써 갔네(요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -네: 멀다 → 머네(요), 살다 → 사네(요). Nouns: -(이)네(요) → 진짜 맛집이네요. Said with a slightly rising, impressed intonation.
endingItems.contrastWith: -네(요) vs -군(요)/구나: both mark realization, but -네 is the everyday, conversational reaction (especially spoken), while -군요/-구나 sounds a touch more bookish or to-oneself ('ah, I see'). Vs plain -아요: 예뻐요 just describes ('it's pretty'); 예쁘네요 adds 'oh, I'm noticing/reacting to this right now.'
sentenceFrames: 생각보다 ___ 네요 (It's more ___ than I thought)

examples.ko: 사진 보니까 거기 단풍 진짜 예쁘네요.
examples.romanization: sajin bonikka geogi danpung jinjja yeppeuneyo.
examples.en: Looking at the photo, the autumn leaves there are really pretty.

examples.ko: 어, 벌써 막차 시간이네. 우리 가야겠다.
examples.romanization: eo, beolsseo makcha siganine. uri gayagetda.
examples.en: Oh, it's already last-train time. We'd better go.
Traffic's clear today — what's the occasion?

examples.ko: 손맛이 좋으시네요! 이거 직접 만드신 거예요?
examples.romanization: sonmasi joeusineyo! igeo jikjeom mandeusin geoyeyo?
examples.en: You're a great cook! Did you make this yourself?

commonMistakes: Using -네요 for facts you already knew — it specifically signals 'I just realized this,' so for known info use plain -아요.
Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 멀네요 is wrong → 머네요; 살네요 → 사네요.

practiceItems.prompt: React to a photo: 'Wow, the view is really nice!' (좋다)
Notice the time: 'Oh, it's already late' (늦다)
React: 'It's farther than I thought' (멀다, ㄹ-drop)

studyOrder: Learn it as your instant 'oh!' reaction to new info or what you see.
Practice the past -았/었네(요) for noticing things already done (벌써 갔네).
Watch the ㄹ-drop (멀다→머네요) and compare lightly with -군요 (more to-oneself).
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -네(요) is the ending you reach for the instant you notice or realize something. See a pretty view and say 예쁘네요!, glance at the clock and say 벌써 늦었네 (oh, it's already late). It carries a warm, spontaneous, slightly impressed feeling, so Koreans use it constantly when reacting to photos, food, or news. The contrast with plain -아요 is subtle but real: 예뻐요 simply states 'it's pretty,' while 예쁘네요 adds 'I'm noticing this right now.' One spelling tip: ㄹ-ending stems drop the ㄹ before -네, so 멀다 becomes 머네요, not 멀네요.

endingItems.title: -geot gata: 'I think / it seems'
endingItems.plainEnglish: You use it to soften an opinion or make a guess — 'I think… / it seems like…' — instead of stating things too directly.
endingItems.whenToUse: Whenever you want to hedge an opinion, prediction, or feeling so you don't sound too blunt. This is everywhere in polite Korean. Example: 이건 좀 어려울 것 같아요. (I think this might be a bit difficult.) Essential for declining, giving feedback at work, and sharing opinions among new acquaintances.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Pick the modifier by tense/type before 것 같다: verbs — past -(으)ㄴ (먹은 것 같다 = seems they ate), present -는 (먹는 것 같다 = seems they're eating), future/guess -(으)ㄹ (먹을 것 같다 = I think they'll eat). Adjectives & 이다 — present -(으)ㄴ (좋은 것 같다, 학생인 것 같다), guess -(으)ㄹ (좋을 것 같다). 것 같다 is often spoken as 것 같아(요) or 거 같아(요). ㄹ-stems and ㅂ/ㄷ irregulars follow the usual modifier rules (살다→사는, 덥다→더운, 듣다→듣는).
endingItems.contrastWith: -것 같다 vs -나 보다: -것 같다 is a broad, soft opinion or guess that can include yourself (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 = I think I caught a cold). -나 보다 is specifically an inference from outside evidence about others/situations (감기 걸렸나 봐 = looks like they caught a cold). Vs flat assertion: 별로예요 ('it's not great') is direct, 별로인 것 같아요 ('I think it's not great') is gentler and safer socially.
sentenceFrames: 이건 좀 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같아요 (I think this might be a bit ___)
그 사람 ___ 는 것 같아 (It seems like they ___)
오늘은 못 ___ (으)ㄹ 것 같은데요 (I don't think I can ___ today…)

examples.ko: 이 옷 나한테 좀 큰 것 같아, 한 사이즈 작은 거 없어요?
examples.romanization: i on nahante jom keun geot gata, han saijeu jageun geo eopseoyo?
examples.en: I think this is a bit big on me — do you have it one size smaller?

examples.ko: 오늘 회식은 못 갈 것 같아요, 집에 일이 좀 있어서요.
examples.romanization: oneul hoesigeun mot gal geot gatayo, jibe iri jom isseoseoyo.
examples.en: I don't think I can make the work dinner today — something came up at home.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 좀 바쁜 것 같더라.
examples.romanization: gyae yojeum jom bappeun geot gatdeora.
examples.en: Seems like they've been pretty busy lately.

examples.ko: 이 정도면 충분할 것 같은데, 어때요?
examples.romanization: i jeongdomyeon chungbunhal geot gateunde, eottaeyo?
examples.en: I think this much should be enough — what do you think?

commonMistakes: Using the wrong modifier tense: 먹는 것 같다 (seems eating now) vs 먹은 것 같다 (seems already ate) vs 먹을 것 같다 (I think will eat) — mixing these changes the meaning.
Over-hedging things you actually know firsthand (나 한국 사람인 것 같아 about yourself sounds odd) — use it for opinions/guesses, not certain facts about yourself.

practiceItems.prompt: Soften an opinion: 'I think this is a bit expensive' (비싸다, present adj)
Politely decline: 'I don't think I can go today' (가다, guess)
Guess about now: 'It seems like it's raining' (오다, present verb)

studyOrder: Learn it first as the all-purpose softener 'I think / it seems.'
Drill the three modifiers before 것: past -(으)ㄴ, present -는 (verbs), future/guess -(으)ㄹ.
Compare with -나 보다 (evidence-based, about others) so you choose the right 'seems.'
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -것 같다 ('I think / it seems') is maybe the most important softening tool in Korean. Koreans avoid sounding too blunt, so instead of 비싸요 (it's expensive) they often say 비싼 것 같아요 (I think it's a bit expensive), and instead of a flat 'no' they say 못 갈 것 같아요 (I don't think I can go). It works for opinions, predictions, and guesses, and it can be about yourself too (나 감기 걸린 것 같아 = I think I caught a cold). The one fiddly part is the little word before 것: use -는 for what's happening now, -(으)ㄴ for what already happened, and -(으)ㄹ for what you predict. In speech it's usually shortened to 거 같아(요).

endingItems.title: -eulgeol: 'I bet…' / 'should've…'
endingItems.plainEnglish: With falling tone it expresses mild regret ('I should have…'); with a guessing tone it makes a confident-ish prediction ('I bet… / probably').
endingItems.whenToUse: Two everyday uses. Regret about something you didn't do: 아, 어제 그거 살걸. (Ugh, I should've bought that yesterday.) Or a hunch you're fairly sure of: 지금 가면 막힐걸? (If we go now, it'll probably be jammed.) Both are very common in casual chat among young adults.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Prediction sense (verbs & adjectives): after a vowel/ㄹ -ㄹ걸(요), after a consonant -을걸(요) → 막히다 → 막힐걸(요), 좋다 → 좋을걸(요), 살다 → 살걸(요). Past prediction: -았/었을걸(요) → 갔을걸요 (they probably went). Regret sense (only your own past inaction, no -요, no past form): -(으)ㄹ걸 → 살걸, 갈걸, 먹을걸 (= I should've bought/gone/eaten). ㄷ-irreg 듣다 → 들을걸, ㅂ-irreg 돕다 → 도울걸. Pronounced [껄].
endingItems.contrastWith: Regret -(으)ㄹ걸 vs -았/었어야 했는데: -ㄹ걸 is the light, spoken 'aw, should've' to yourself; -았어야 했는데 is a fuller 'I really should have…'. Prediction -(으)ㄹ걸(요)? vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: -ㄹ걸 is a softer hunch you're guessing ('probably, I bet'), -ㄹ 거예요 states a more confident future. Tone tells regret (falling) from prediction (slight rise).
sentenceFrames: 지금 ___ 면 ___ 을걸? (If we ___ now, it'll probably ___)

examples.ko: 아, 어제 표 미리 예매할걸. 지금 다 매진이래.
examples.romanization: a, eoje pyo miri yemaehalgeol. jigeum da maejinirae.
examples.en: Ugh, I should've booked the tickets yesterday. They say it's all sold out now.
If we leave now, it'll probably be super jammed, I bet.
They'll probably be happy to hear that, I'd bet.
I should've just stayed home — coming out was pointless.

commonMistakes: Using the regret -(으)ㄹ걸 about someone else — it's only for your OWN past inaction; for predictions about others use -(으)ㄹ걸요? with a guessing tone.
Adding -요 or past tense to the regret meaning (살걸요 / 샀을걸 as regret is wrong) — regret stays plain present-shaped -(으)ㄹ걸; -요 and -았을걸 push it into the prediction reading.

practiceItems.prompt: Express regret: 'Ugh, I should've left earlier' (일찍 나오다)
Make a hunch: 'That place is probably closed now' (문 닫다)

studyOrder: Learn the two senses separately: falling-tone regret ('should've') and guessing-tone prediction ('I bet').
For regret, lock in: your own past inaction only, plain -(으)ㄹ걸, no -요.
For prediction, practice -(으)ㄹ걸요? and the past -았/었을걸(요), and contrast with the firmer -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: -(으)ㄹ걸 wears two hats depending on your tone. Said with a sighing, falling tone, it's regret — 'I should've': 일찍 나올걸 (I should've left earlier), 그거 살걸 (I should've bought that). Said with a slight upward, guessing tone, it's a confident hunch — 'I bet / probably': 지금 가면 막힐걸? (it'll probably be jammed if we go now). Young Koreans use both constantly in chat. Two things to remember: the regret version is only about your own past inaction and stays plain (no -요), while the prediction version can add -요 to be polite (비쌀걸요) and can go past tense (갔을걸 = they probably went). It's spelled 걸 but sounds like '껄'.

endingItems.title: Reported statement: said that
endingItems.plainEnglish: It relays what someone else said as a statement, like English said that.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to pass on what a person told you, in texts, gossip, or office updates. Example: 팀장님이 회의가 30분 늦어진다고 했어요 (The team lead said the meeting is pushed back 30 minutes).
endingItems.attachmentRule: For a present-tense verb add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel stem (가다→간다고) and -는다고 after a consonant stem (먹다→먹는다고). Adjectives and 있다/없다 just add -다고 (춥다→춥다고, 재미있다→재미있다고). Past tense uses -았/었다고 (갔다고, 먹었다고). A noun takes -(이)라고 (학생이라고, 친구라고). 하다 is usually said as 했어요 (said) or 한다고/하더라고 in retelling.
endingItems.contrastWith: -다고 하다 reports a plain statement, while -냐고 하다 reports a question and -(으)라고 하다 reports a command, so match the ending to the kind of sentence you are relaying.

examples.en: My girlfriend said she is a bit tired today.
The team lead said the meeting will be 30 minutes late.

examples.ko: 집주인이 다음 달부터 월세 올린다고 했어요.
examples.romanization: jipjuini daeum dalbuteo wolse ollindago haesseoyo.
examples.en: The landlord said he will raise the rent starting next month.

examples.ko: 걔가 어제 그 카페 진짜 맛있었다고 했어.
examples.romanization: gyaega eoje geu kape jinjja masisseotdago haesseo.
examples.en: She said that cafe was really good yesterday.

commonMistakes: Using the plain polite form before -다고, like 가요고 하다; you must use the plain stem form, so it is 간다고 해요, not 가요고 해요.
Forgetting the verb vs adjective split: verbs need -ㄴ다고/-는다고 (먹는다고), but adjectives just take -다고 (춥다고), so 춥는다고 is wrong.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend said he is coming tomorrow.
She said the food was delicious. (past)
The boss said he is busy.

studyOrder: Decide if the relayed sentence is a verb, adjective, or noun
Verbs: add -ㄴ다고 after a vowel, -는다고 after a consonant
Adjectives and 있다/없다: just add -다고; nouns add -(이)라고
Finish with 하다, usually 했어요 to mean someone said
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-다고 하다 is how Korean relays what someone said, the way English uses said that. The tricky part is the front ending, because present-tense verbs do not keep the polite -요 form; instead they switch to the plain shape, so 가다 becomes 간다고 and 먹다 becomes 먹는다고. Adjectives are easier and simply add -다고, as in 피곤하다고 (said she is tired), and past tense for everything is -았/었다고 (맛있었다고). You will hear this constantly in real life: 팀장님이 회의 늦는다고 했어요 passes on the boss's message, and 친구가 내일 온다고 했어요 reports a friend's plan. The number one beginner slip is gluing -다고 onto the polite form, so remember it is 간다고 해요, never 가요고 해요.

endingItems.title: Reported question: asked whether
endingItems.plainEnglish: It relays a question that someone else asked, like English asked whether or asked if.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to pass on a question another person asked you or someone else. Example: 친구가 주말에 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요 (My friend asked if I have time this weekend).
endingItems.attachmentRule: In everyday speech add -냐고 to the plain stem of verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike (가냐고, 먹냐고, 바쁘냐고, 있냐고). Past tense uses -았/었냐고 (갔냐고, 먹었냐고). A noun takes -(이)냐고 (학생이냐고, 누구냐고). The reporting verb is usually 물어봤어요 (asked) or 했어요. The fuller written forms 가느냐고/먹느냐고 also exist but sound stiff in speech.
endingItems.contrastWith: -냐고 하다 reports a question, while -다고 하다 reports a plain statement; if the original sentence had a question mark, use -냐고.

examples.en: My friend asked if I have time this weekend.

examples.ko: 면접관이 왜 우리 회사에 지원했냐고 물어봤어요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeopgwani wae uri hoesae jiwonhaennyago mureobwasseoyo.
examples.en: The interviewer asked why I applied to our company.
The girl I'm into asked me if I have a girlfriend.
My mom asked whether I had eaten.

commonMistakes: Using -다고 for a relayed question, like 시간 있다고 물어봤어요; a reported question needs -냐고, so it is 시간 있냐고 물어봤어요.
Keeping the polite -요 before -냐고, like 가요냐고; attach -냐고 to the plain stem, so 가냐고, not 가요냐고.

practiceItems.prompt: My friend asked if I'm coming.
He asked if it was expensive. (past)
She asked who that person is.

studyOrder: Confirm the original sentence was a question
Add -냐고 to the plain stem of the verb or adjective
Use -았/었냐고 for past and -(이)냐고 for nouns
Finish with 물어봤어요 or 했어요 to mean someone asked
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-냐고 하다 relays a question that someone asked, matching English asked if or asked whether. The big convenience is that modern spoken Korean uses one ending, -냐고, for verbs, adjectives, and 있다/없다 alike, so you say 가냐고 (asked if I go), 바쁘냐고 (asked if I'm busy), and 시간 있냐고 (asked if I have time) all the same way. Past questions use -았/었냐고, as in 밥 먹었냐고 했어요 (asked whether I ate). The reporting verb is most naturally 물어봤어요, literally tried asking, which sounds warm and conversational. Beginners often reuse -다고 here, but that ending is only for statements; if the original had a question mark, switch to -냐고, so 여자친구 있냐고 물어봤어, not 있다고.

endingItems.title: Worried that / afraid that
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you do something because you are worried or afraid that an unwanted thing might happen.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to give an anxious reason for an action. Example: 지각할까 봐 택시 탔어요 (I took a taxi because I was worried I'd be late).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Add -ㄹ까 봐 to a vowel-ending stem (가다→갈까 봐, 오다→올까 봐) and -을까 봐 to a consonant-ending stem (늦다→늦을까 봐, 먹다→먹을까 봐). For a worry about something already past, use -았/었을까 봐 (실수했을까 봐). The main clause is your reaction, often ending in a past action you took. The full form 봐요 is more polite; 봐 is casual.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 gives a worried reason, while -(으)니까 gives a neutral, factual reason; use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 only when there is real worry or fear about a bad outcome.

examples.ko: 길 막힐까 봐 한 시간 일찍 나왔어요.
examples.romanization: gil makilkka bwa han sigan iljjing nawasseoyo.
examples.en: I left an hour early because I was worried traffic would be bad.
I'm so nervous because I'm afraid I'll fail the interview.
I kept checking because I was afraid my message had been ignored.
I packed an umbrella in case it rains.

commonMistakes: Using it for a neutral reason instead of a worry, like 배고플까 봐 먹어요 to just mean because I'm hungry; use -(으)니까 unless there is real worry.
Forgetting the consonant linker, like saying 늦까 봐 instead of the correct 늦을까 봐.

practiceItems.prompt: I left early because I was worried I'd be late.
I packed extra because I was afraid it wouldn't be enough.

studyOrder: Identify the bad outcome you are worried about
Add -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel or -을까 봐 after a consonant
Use -았/었을까 봐 if the worry is about something past
State the action you took in the main clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐 is the phrase Koreans use when worry drives an action, roughly worried that or afraid that. The structure is worry first, action second: 지각할까 봐 택시 탔어요 means I took a taxi because I was afraid I'd be late, and 비 올까 봐 우산 챙겼어요 means I packed an umbrella in case it rains. Attachment is the usual split, -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel and -을까 봐 after a consonant, so 늦다 becomes 늦을까 봐. The key feeling is anxiety about a bad result, which is what separates it from the neutral reason marker -(으)니까; you would not use 배고플까 봐 just to say you're hungry. In casual texting you'll see the short 봐, but 봐요 sounds more polite when you talk to someone senior.

endingItems.title: It seems / I think
endingItems.plainEnglish: It softens a statement into a guess or impression, like English it seems or I think.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to give a soft opinion or a guess instead of a flat assertion. Example: 그 식당 오늘 문 닫은 것 같아요 (That restaurant seems to be closed today).
endingItems.attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 것 같다 (가다→가는 것 같다, 먹다→먹는 것 같다). For a present adjective add -은 것 같다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 것 같다 after a vowel (춥다→추운 것 같다, 크다→큰 것 같다). Past uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (간 것 같다, 먹은 것 같다) and future uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (갈 것 같다). 것 is often spoken as 거, giving 가는 거 같아요.
endingItems.contrastWith: -는 것 같다 is a soft personal guess, while -겠- and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 lean toward prediction; Koreans use -는 것 같다 constantly to sound modest rather than too certain.

examples.ko: 이 카페 사람이 너무 많은 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: i kape sarami neomu maneun geot gatayo.
examples.en: This cafe seems to have too many people.

examples.ko: 걔 요즘 좀 바쁜 것 같아.
examples.romanization: gyae yojeum jom bappeun geot gata.
examples.en: She seems kind of busy these days.
I think the delivery is going to be a bit late.

examples.ko: 어제 비 온 것 같아요. 길이 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: eoje bi on geot gatayo. giri da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: It seems it rained yesterday. The roads are all wet.

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 것 같다 on an adjective, like 바쁘는 것 같다; adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같다, so 바쁜 것 같다.
Confusing the tense modifier: 가는 것 같다 is present (seems to go), but 간 것 같다 is past (seems to have gone).

practiceItems.prompt: It seems like it's going to rain. (future)

studyOrder: Decide if the word is a verb or an adjective
Pick the tense: present, past -(으)ㄴ, or future -(으)ㄹ
Build the right modifier, e.g. 가는 / 간 / 갈
Add 것 같다 (or spoken 거 같아요) to mean it seems
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: A/V-는 것 같다 is the everyday way Koreans soften what they say into a guess, like it seems or I think. It is everywhere in real conversation because stating things too bluntly can sound arrogant, so 그 식당 닫은 것 같아요 (it seems the place is closed) feels more natural than a flat assertion. The form rides on Korean's modifier endings: present verbs use -는 것 같다 (가는 것 같다), present adjectives use -은/-ㄴ 것 같다 (바쁜 것 같다), the past uses -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (간 것 같다), and the future uses -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (올 것 같다). In speech 것 almost always shrinks to 거, so you'll hear 가는 거 같아요. Two pitfalls: do not put the verb ending -는 on an adjective, and watch the tense modifier, since 가는 것 같다 and 간 것 같다 mean different things.

endingItems.title: Decide to / agree to
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you decided or agreed to do something, often a plan with yourself or others.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to announce a decision or a mutual plan. Example: 우리 다음 주에 만나기로 했어요 (We decided to meet next week).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -기로 하다 to the plain verb stem with no vowel or consonant change at all (가다→가기로 하다, 먹다→먹기로 하다, 운동하다→운동하기로 하다). The decision is usually reported in the past as -기로 했어요 (decided), since the choice is already made. To express a firm resolution you can say -기로 마음먹었어요. Negative is -지 않기로 하다 (안 가기로 했어요).
endingItems.contrastWith: -기로 하다 marks a settled decision or agreement, while -(으)ㄹ게요 is an on-the-spot promise to the listener; use -기로 했어요 to report a plan you already locked in.

examples.en: I decided to quit smoking starting this year.
We decided to meet at the Han River this weekend.

examples.ko: 돈 모으려고 당분간 택시 안 타기로 했어.
examples.romanization: don moeuryeogo dangbungan taeksi an tagiro haesseo.
examples.en: To save money, I decided not to take taxis for a while.
We decided to have a meeting with the team every Friday.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기로, like 가아기로 하다; always use the plain stem, so 가기로 하다.
Using the present 하다 when the decision is already settled; a finished decision is normally -기로 했어요, not -기로 해요.

practiceItems.prompt: We decided to meet next week.

studyOrder: Identify the action you decided on
Take the plain verb stem with no change
Add -기로 하다, usually as -기로 했어요
For a negative decision use -지 않기로 or 안 ...-기로
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-기로 하다 is how you announce a decision or a plan you've agreed on, and it is pleasantly regular because you just add -기로 하다 to the bare verb stem, no spelling changes. Because a decision is normally already made by the time you mention it, the natural form is the past -기로 했어요, so 우리 다음 주에 만나기로 했어요 means we decided to meet next week and 담배 끊기로 했어요 means I decided to quit smoking. It works for solo resolutions and for group agreements equally well. For a decision not to do something, slot in the negative: 안 가기로 했어요 or 가지 않기로 했어요. Keep it apart from -(으)ㄹ게요, which is a promise you make to someone right now; -기로 했어요 reports a plan you already settled.

endingItems.title: Pretend to / act like
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says someone pretends or fakes doing or being something.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when a person acts a certain way without it being true. Example: 상사 와서 일하는 척했어요 (My boss came so I pretended to work).
endingItems.attachmentRule: For a present verb add -는 척하다 (자다→자는 척하다, 먹다→먹는 척하다). For an adjective add -은 척하다 after a consonant and -ㄴ 척하다 after a vowel (아프다→아픈 척하다, 바쁘다→바쁜 척하다). Past action uses the -(으)ㄴ modifier (안 들은 척하다 = pretend not to have heard). You may also see 체하다, which means the same thing.
endingItems.contrastWith: -는 척하다 means faking something that is not real, while -는 것 같다 means it genuinely seems true to you; the first is deliberate pretense, the second is an honest guess.

examples.en: My boss came so I pretended to be working hard.

examples.ko: 전 남친 마주쳤는데 그냥 못 본 척했어.
examples.romanization: jeon namchin majuchyeonneunde geunyang mot bon cheokaesseo.
examples.en: I ran into my ex but I just pretended not to see him.
I pretended to be sick to skip the company dinner.
She totally knows but acts like she doesn't, you know.

commonMistakes: Using the verb ending -는 척하다 on an adjective, like 아프는 척하다; adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 척하다, so 아픈 척하다.
Confusing it with -는 것 같다: 자는 척하다 means pretending to sleep, but 자는 것 같다 means it seems she is sleeping.

practiceItems.prompt: I pretended not to hear. (past action)

studyOrder: Decide if the pretense is a verb or an adjective
Verbs: present -는 척, past action -(으)ㄴ 척
Adjectives: -은 척 after a consonant, -ㄴ 척 after a vowel
Add 척하다 and conjugate it for your tense
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-는 척하다 means to pretend or fake, and it shows up a lot in stories about work, dating, and saving face. The form uses Korean's modifier endings: a present verb takes -는 척하다 (자는 척하다 = pretend to sleep, 일하는 척하다 = pretend to work), an adjective takes -은/-ㄴ 척하다 (아픈 척하다 = pretend to be sick), and a past action takes -(으)ㄴ 척하다, as in 못 본 척했어 (pretended not to see). A super common real-life line is 상사 와서 일하는 척했어요, which any office worker will recognize. The classic mistake is treating it like -는 것 같다; but those are opposites in spirit, since 척하다 is deliberate faking while 것 같다 is an honest impression, so 자는 척하다 (pretending to sleep) is very different from 자는 것 같다 (seems to be sleeping).

endingItems.title: Switching mid-action
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you were doing one action and then, partway through, switched to or were interrupted by another.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when you stop one action partway and move to a second one, often unexpectedly. Example: 집에 가다가 편의점에 들렀어요 (I was on my way home and stopped by the convenience store).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -다가 (often shortened to -다) straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (가다→가다가, 먹다→먹다가, 보다→보다가). The subject of both clauses must be the same person, and the first action is left unfinished. For a finished action that then leads to a result, you can use the past stem -았/었다가 (갔다가 = went and then came back).
endingItems.contrastWith: -다가 means you cut one action short to do another, while -고 나서 means you fully finish the first action before starting the second.

examples.en: I was on my way home and ran into a friend.
I was watching a drama and fell asleep.
I was working and suddenly got a headache.
I was riding the bus and got motion sick.

commonMistakes: Using -다가 with two different subjects; both actions must be done by the same person.
Conjugating the verb before -다가, like 먹어다가; attach it to the plain stem, so 먹다가.

practiceItems.prompt: I was going home and (met a friend)
I was watching a drama and (fell asleep)
I was working and (suddenly got a headache)

studyOrder: Find the first action you start but do not finish
Attach -다가 to its plain stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
Add the new or interrupting action in the second clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-다가 captures that very common moment when you are in the middle of doing something and then switch to, or get interrupted by, something else. You simply glue -다가 (you will often hear it cut to just -다) onto the plain verb stem, so 가다 becomes 가다가 and 보다 becomes 보다가. A picture helps: 집에 가다가 친구를 만났어요 means I was heading home and ran into a friend along the way, with the first action left hanging. Two rules keep it natural: the same person must do both actions, and you attach it to the bare stem, never a conjugated form like 먹어다가. Compare it with -고 나서, where you completely finish the first action before moving on, whereas -다가 cuts the first action short.

endingItems.title: Because of (sudden, bad) cause
endingItems.plainEnglish: It gives a sudden or unintended reason that caused an unwanted result.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to blame an unexpected action or event for a negative outcome. Example: 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지하철을 놓쳤어요 (I overslept, so I missed the subway).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -는 바람에 to a verb stem (자다→자는 바람에, 막히다→막히는 바람에). It only goes on action verbs, not adjectives, and even though it describes a past result you keep the form as -는 바람에, not a past form. The result clause is almost always negative or unplanned and is normally in the past tense.
endingItems.contrastWith: -는 바람에 blames a sudden, usually bad and unintended cause, while -아/어서 is a neutral all-purpose because that works for good or bad results alike.

examples.en: I overslept, so I was late to work.
The traffic was jammed, so I was late to my appointment.

examples.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
examples.romanization: gapjagi biga oneun barame da jeojeosseoyo.
examples.en: It suddenly rained, so I got soaked.
The person next to me shoved me, so I fell over.

commonMistakes: Attaching it to an adjective, like 바쁜 바람에; it goes only on action verbs.
Putting it on a past stem, like 잤는 바람에; keep it as the present -는 바람에 even when the result is past.

practiceItems.prompt: I overslept, so (I was late to work)
the traffic was jammed, so (I was late)
it suddenly rained, so (I got soaked)
practiceItems.ko: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.
practiceItems.answer: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 다 젖었어요.

studyOrder: Find the sudden action or event that caused trouble
Attach -는 바람에 to its verb stem
Keep it in the -는 form even for a past result
State the negative or unplanned result in the past tense
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-는 바람에 is the connector you reach for when something unexpected goes wrong and you want to pin the blame on its cause. You add -는 바람에 to an action verb stem, so 자다 becomes 자는 바람에 and 막히다 becomes 막히는 바람에. The feel is always a sudden, usually unwanted cause leading to a bad result, as in 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지각했어요 (I overslept, so I was late). Two things trip learners up: it only attaches to action verbs, not adjectives, so 바쁜 바람에 is wrong; and even though the result already happened, you keep the present shape 자는 바람에, not 잤는 바람에. Think of it as a more dramatic, blame-assigning cousin of the plain because connector 아/어서.

endingItems.title: I noticed X, then Y
endingItems.plainEnglish: It links something you personally observed earlier to a result or change that followed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to report that you watched someone do or be something, and then a related outcome happened. Example: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 (My brother kept eating late-night snacks, and then he gained weight).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -더니 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (먹다→먹더니, 춥다→춥더니). For the typical use, the first clause is something you observed about another person or the weather, and the second clause is its natural result. With your own actions, the related form -았/었더니 (먹었더니) is used to mean after I did X, then Y happened.
endingItems.contrastWith: -더니 reports a result you observed following someone else's past action, while -아/어서 simply gives a neutral cause without that sense of personal observation and contrast.

examples.ko: 동생이 매일 게임만 하더니 시험을 망쳤어요.
examples.romanization: dongsaengi maeil geimman hadeoni siheomeul mangchyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My brother did nothing but game every day, and then he bombed the exam.
The weather was cold earlier, but now it is warm.

examples.ko: 친구가 한국어를 열심히 배우더니 이제 정말 잘해요.
examples.romanization: chinguga hangugeoreul yeolsimhi baeudeoni ije jeongmal jalhaeyo.
examples.en: My friend studied Korean hard, and now she is really good at it.
The sky got cloudy, and then it started to rain.

commonMistakes: Using -더니 about your own present feelings; for plain first-person statements it sounds off, and -았/었더니 fits self-actions better.
Adding vowel harmony before -더니, like 먹어더니; attach it straight to the stem, so 먹더니.

practiceItems.prompt: he only gamed every day, and then (he bombed the exam)
it was cold earlier, but now (it is warm)
the sky got cloudy, and then (it started to rain)

studyOrder: Recall something you personally observed earlier
Attach -더니 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause the result or change that followed
For your own actions, switch to -았/었더니 instead
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V/A-더니 is how Korean ties together something you watched happen and the result or change that came after it, with a built-in sense of I saw this myself. You attach -더니 to the plain stem, so 먹다 becomes 먹더니 and 춥다 becomes 춥더니. It shines when describing other people or the weather: 동생이 매일 야식을 먹더니 살이 쪘어요 means my brother kept eating late-night snacks, and sure enough he gained weight. It can also mark a contrast over time, as in 아까는 춥더니 지금은 따뜻해요 (it was cold earlier, but now it is warm). The catch for beginners is the person: -더니 fits things you observed about others, while for your own actions you switch to -았/었더니, as in 운동했더니 다리가 아파요 (I worked out, and now my legs hurt).

endingItems.title: Since I noticed, so I…
endingItems.plainEnglish: It gives the reason you noticed that made you spontaneously do something yourself.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when something you saw or heard prompted you to take an action on the spot. Example: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 (The strawberries were cheap, so I bought some).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -길래 to the plain stem of a verb or adjective with no vowel change (싸다→싸길래, 울다→울길래, 먹다→먹길래). The first clause is the reason you perceived, and the second clause must be your own action and is usually in the past. For a noun reason use N(이)길래.
endingItems.contrastWith: -길래 is a spoken, reason-based because that leads to your own spontaneous reaction, while -으니까 is a broader because that can also justify commands and suggestions, which -길래 cannot.

examples.en: The strawberries were cheap, so I bought two packs.
The child was crying, so I picked her up.
The weather was nice, so I came out for a walk.
My friend said it was delicious, so I ordered it too.

commonMistakes: Using a command or suggestion in the second clause, like ...길래 사세요; the result must be your own action, not an order to someone else.
Putting your own planned action as the reason; the first clause should be something you observed, not your own decision.

practiceItems.prompt: the strawberries were cheap, so (I bought two packs)
the child was crying, so (I picked her up)
the weather was nice, so (I came out for a walk)

studyOrder: Find what you saw or heard that prompted you
Attach -길래 to that verb or adjective stem
Make the second clause your own reaction
Usually put your reaction in the past tense
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V/A-길래 is a friendly, spoken connector that explains the reason you noticed which pushed you to do something yourself, on the spot. You add -길래 straight to the stem, so 싸다 becomes 싸길래 and 울다 becomes 울길래. The classic shape is observation then my reaction: 딸기가 싸길래 좀 샀어요 means the strawberries looked cheap, so I went ahead and bought some. The key restriction is that the second clause has to be your own action, very often in the past tense, so you cannot end with a command like 사세요. Think of it as warmer and more conversational than 으니까, and remember that 으니까 can justify suggestions and orders while 길래 only explains what made you, the speaker, act.

endingItems.title: The more, the more
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says as one thing increases, another thing changes along with it.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for the more X, the more Y patterns. Example: 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Add -을수록 to a stem ending in a consonant (먹다→먹을수록, 작다→작을수록) and -ㄹ수록 to a stem ending in a vowel (가다→갈수록, 크다→클수록). ㄹ-stems drop their ㄹ and take -ㄹ수록 (살다→살수록, 멀다→멀수록). It is very often paired with -(으)면 in front for emphasis, as in 보면 볼수록.
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ수록 means the more of one thing brings more of another, a sliding scale, while -(으)니까 simply states a cause and effect without that increasing-together feeling.

examples.en: The more I study Korean, the more fun it gets.
The more I listen to this song, the more I like it.
The more people there are, the louder it gets.
The more I read this book, the harder it gets.

commonMistakes: Using -을수록 after a vowel stem, like 갈을수록; vowel stems take -ㄹ수록, so 갈수록.
Spacing it wrong as -ㄹ 수록; write 수록 attached, as in 할수록, not 할 수록.

practiceItems.prompt: the more I study Korean, (the more fun it gets)
the more I listen to this song, (the more I like it)
the more people there are, (the louder it gets)

studyOrder: Find the thing that increases
Add -을수록 after a consonant or -ㄹ수록 after a vowel
Optionally add -(으)면 in front for emphasis
Put the matching change in the second clause, often with 더
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V/A-(으)ㄹ수록 is the Korean version of the more, the more, describing how two things rise or change together on a sliding scale. The attachment follows the usual sound split: consonant stems take -을수록 (먹을수록, 작을수록) and vowel stems take -ㄹ수록 (갈수록, 클수록), while ㄹ-stems drop the ㄹ first (살수록). A natural example is 한국어는 공부할수록 재미있어요 (the more you study Korean, the more fun it becomes), and Koreans love to double it up with -(으)면, as in 보면 볼수록 (the more you look). Two pitfalls: do not use -을수록 after a vowel, so it is 갈수록 not 갈을수록; and write 수록 right onto the verb, never spaced as 할 수록. Adding 더 (more) in the second clause makes the rising effect even clearer.

endingItems.title: In order to
endingItems.plainEnglish: It states the purpose or goal you are doing the main action for.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for in order to do something, especially deliberate goals. Example: 살을 빼기 위해서 매일 운동해요 (I exercise every day in order to lose weight).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -기 위해서 (or the slightly more formal -기 위하여) to the plain verb stem with no change (빼다→빼기 위해서, 사다→사기 위해서). 위해 and 위해서 are interchangeable. For a noun goal, use N을/를 위해서 instead (가족을 위해서 = for my family). The subject usually intends the goal on purpose.
endingItems.contrastWith: -기 위해서 expresses a deliberate purpose with an action verb goal, while -(으)러 also means in order to but only attaches to motion plans with 가다/오다, whereas 위해서 works with almost any main verb.

examples.en: I exercise every day in order to lose weight.

examples.ko: 한국 회사에 취직하기 위해서 한국어를 배워요.
examples.romanization: hangu koesae chwijikagi wihaeseo hangugeoreul baewoyo.
examples.en: I am learning Korean in order to get a job at a Korean company.
I cut back on eating out in order to save money.
I quit smoking for the sake of my health.

commonMistakes: Conjugating the verb before -기 위해서, like 빼서 위해서; use the plain stem plus -기, so 빼기 위해서.
Using -기 위해서 with a noun; for nouns drop -기 and say N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서, not 가족기 위해서.

practiceItems.prompt: in order to lose weight (I exercise every day)
in order to save money (I cut back on eating out)
for the sake of my health (I quit smoking)

studyOrder: Decide the goal or purpose you are aiming for
If it is an action, add -기 위해서 to that verb stem
If it is a noun, use N을/를 위해서 instead
Put the action you take toward that goal in the main clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-기 위해(서) is the clear, slightly formal way to state the purpose behind what you do, matching English in order to. For an action goal you add -기 위해서 to the plain stem, so 빼다 becomes 빼기 위해서 in 살을 빼기 위해서 운동해요 (I exercise in order to lose weight); 위해 and 위해서 mean the same thing. When the goal is a noun, you switch to N을/를 위해서, as in 가족을 위해서 (for my family), so do not jam 기 onto a noun. The most common slip is conjugating the verb first, like 빼서 위해서; always keep the bare stem plus 기. Compare it with -(으)러, which also means in order to but only pairs with going and coming verbs, while 기 위해서 works with nearly any main verb and stresses a deliberate goal.

endingItems.title: Because / and then
endingItems.plainEnglish: It links a cause to its result, or one action to the next closely connected one.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to give a reason, or to show one action leading right into another with the same subject. Example: 늦어서 택시를 탔어요 (I was late, so I took a taxi).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Build the 아/어 connective by vowel harmony: if the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ use -아서 (가다→가서, 좋다→좋아서), otherwise use -어서 (먹다→먹어서, 늦다→늦어서); 하다 becomes 해서. Crucially, the first clause never takes a tense marker, so you say 늦어서, never 늦었어서, and you cannot use a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서.
endingItems.contrastWith: -아/어서 gives a tight cause-result where the first clause stays tenseless and cannot lead to a command, while -(으)니까 is a because that allows commands and suggestions and can carry tense.

examples.en: I was hungry, so I made ramyeon.
The road was slippery, so I walked carefully.
I met my friend and we had coffee together.
I caught a cold, so I could not go to work.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 늦었어서; keep it tenseless as 늦어서 and mark tense only at the end.
Using a command or suggestion after a reason -아/어서, like 피곤해서 쉬세요; for that use -(으)니까 instead.

practiceItems.prompt: I was hungry, so (I made ramyeon)
the road was slippery, so (I walked carefully)
I caught a cold, so (I could not go to work)

studyOrder: Find the cause or the first action
Make the 아/어 connective using vowel harmony
Keep that first clause tenseless
Add the result or next action, marking tense only at the end
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V/A-아/어서 is one of the most useful connectors in Korean, covering both because and a smooth and then between two linked actions. You form it with the same vowel harmony as the present tense: ㅏ or ㅗ stems take -아서 (가서, 좋아서), other stems take -어서 (먹어서, 늦어서), and 하다 becomes 해서. So 배가 고파서 라면을 끓였어요 means I was hungry, so I made ramyeon. Two rules are essential. First, the 아/어서 clause stays tenseless; you mark past or future only on the final verb, so it is 늦어서, never 늦었어서. Second, you cannot follow a reason 아/어서 with a command or suggestion, so for telling someone to rest because they are tired you must switch to 피곤하니까 쉬세요 using 으니까 instead.

endingItems.title: As soon as
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says the second action happens immediately after the first one finishes.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it for as soon as one thing happens, another follows right away. Example: 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (As soon as I got home, I lay down on the bed).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -자마자 straight to the plain verb stem with no vowel change and regardless of consonant or vowel ending (오다→오자마자, 끝나다→끝나자마자, 받다→받자마자). It goes only on action verbs. The first clause carries no tense marker; the tense is shown on the final verb.
endingItems.contrastWith: -자마자 stresses an immediate, back-to-back sequence with almost no gap, while -고 나서 means after finishing, allowing a normal gap of time between the two actions.

examples.en: As soon as I got home, I washed my hands.
As soon as the alarm rang, I got up.
As soon as class ended, I went straight home.
As soon as I got my paycheck, I spent it all.

commonMistakes: Putting tense on the first clause, like 왔자마자; attach -자마자 to the plain stem, so 오자마자.
Using it for actions with a long gap between them; for that meaning use -고 나서, not -자마자.

practiceItems.prompt: as soon as I got home (I washed my hands)
as soon as the alarm rang (I got up)
as soon as class ended (I went straight home)

studyOrder: Find the first action that triggers the next
Attach -자마자 to its plain stem
Keep the first clause tenseless
Put the immediate next action in the second clause, often with 바로
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-자마자 expresses that the moment one action finishes, the next one happens, just like English as soon as. It is wonderfully simple to attach: add -자마자 to the plain verb stem with no changes for vowels or consonants, so 오다 becomes 오자마자 and 받다 becomes 받자마자. A natural example is 집에 오자마자 침대에 누웠어요 (the second I got home, I flopped onto the bed). Keep the first clause tenseless and mark tense only at the end, so write 오자마자, not 왔자마자. The nuance is immediacy with essentially no gap, which is why you often add 바로 (right away); when there is a normal pause between the two actions, use -고 나서 instead to mean simply after finishing.

endingItems.title: So that / until
endingItems.plainEnglish: It sets a goal or limit that the main action aims toward, often so that something happens.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to do an action so that a result is reached, or to do something up to a point. Example: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 (I dress warmly so that I don't catch a cold).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -도록 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change (늦다→늦도록, 알다→알도록, 들리다→들리도록). It commonly appears in the negative as -지 않도록 (so that ... not) and in advice or instructions. It can also mean until a point, as in 밤늦도록 (until late at night).
endingItems.contrastWith: -도록 sets an aim or limit so that something is achieved, while -기 위해서 states a deliberate purpose; -도록 often points at a result or standard to keep, including not letting something happen.

examples.ko: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.

examples.en: Please speak loudly so that others can hear well.

examples.romanization: gamgie geolliji antorok oseul ttatteutage ibeuseyo.
examples.en: Dress warmly so that you do not catch a cold.
I made a note so that I would not forget.
I worked until late last night.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before -도록, like 듣어도록; attach it to the plain stem, so 듣도록.
Forgetting the natural negative shape -지 않도록 for so that ... not, like saying 안 늦도록 instead of 늦지 않도록.

practiceItems.answer: 다른 사람들이 잘 듣도록 크게 말해 주세요.

practiceItems.answer: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입으세요.

studyOrder: Decide the result or limit you are aiming for
Attach -도록 to the verb stem
Use -지 않도록 when the goal is to prevent something
Put the action that works toward it in the main clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-도록 marks the goal, standard, or limit that your main action is reaching toward, and it is everywhere in advice and instructions. You attach -도록 to the plain verb stem, so 듣다 becomes 듣도록 and 늦다 becomes 늦도록. Often the aim is to prevent something, which shows up as the negative -지 않도록: 감기에 걸리지 않도록 옷을 따뜻하게 입어요 means I dress warmly so that I do not catch a cold. It can also mark a time limit meaning until, as in 밤늦도록 일했어요 (I worked until late at night). Two tips: attach it to the bare stem, not a harmonized form like 듣어도록; and for so that not, prefer the smooth 지 않도록 over patching 안 in front. It overlaps with 기 위해서 but leans toward a result or rule you want to keep.

endingItems.title: Busy doing, so couldn't
endingItems.plainEnglish: It gives a time- or effort-consuming action as the reason you could not do something else.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it when being busy with one action caused a negative result, like not finishing or being unable to do another. Example: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 (I was busy watching a drama, so I couldn't do my homework).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -느라(고) to an action verb stem with no vowel change (보다→보느라고, 일하다→일하느라고, 자다→자느라고); -느라 and -느라고 are interchangeable. The same person must do both actions, it goes only on action verbs, and the second clause is normally negative or apologetic. Do not add a tense marker before it.
endingItems.contrastWith: -느라(고) blames a time- or effort-consuming action for a negative result with the same subject, while -아/어서 is a neutral because that allows positive results and different subjects too.

examples.en: I was busy gaming, so I missed your call.
I was busy with my part-time job, so I had no time to study.
I was busy looking after the kid, so I could not sleep a wink.
I was busy waiting for the bus, so I was late.

commonMistakes: Using it with an adjective or with two different subjects; it needs the same person doing an action verb.
Pairing it with a positive, happy result; the second clause should be a negative or unable outcome, so avoid things like 보느라고 행복했어요.

practiceItems.prompt: I was busy gaming, so (I missed your call)
I was busy with my part-time job, so (I had no time to study)
I was busy waiting for the bus, so (I was late)

studyOrder: Find the action that ate up your time or energy
Attach -느라(고) to that action verb stem
Make sure the same person does both actions
State the negative result, often with 못 or 안, in the second clause
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-느라(고) explains that you were tied up doing one thing, and that is why something else did not get done. You attach -느라고 (or just -느라) to an action verb stem, so 보다 becomes 보느라고 and 일하다 becomes 일하느라고. The feel is always an excuse for a negative outcome with one subject: 드라마를 보느라고 숙제를 못 했어요 means I was busy watching a drama, so I could not do my homework. Three things keep it correct: it attaches only to action verbs, both actions must be done by the same person, and the result clause should be negative or apologetic, frequently with 못 or 안. That negative-result requirement is what separates it from the all-purpose 아/어서, which happily allows good results and different subjects.

endingItems.title: After finishing
endingItems.plainEnglish: It says you completely finish one action before starting the next.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use it to stress that the first action is fully done, then you move on. Example: 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat).
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no vowel change for both vowel and consonant endings (먹다→먹고 나서, 씻다→씻고 나서, 하다→하고 나서). It goes on action verbs only, since it implies completion. The tense is marked on the final verb, not on the -고 나서 clause.
endingItems.contrastWith: -고 나서 highlights that the first action is fully completed before the next, while plain -고 just lists or sequences actions without stressing completion, and -다가 means you stopped the first action partway.

examples.en: I worked out and then took a shower.

examples.romanization: babeul meokgo naseo yageul meogeoya haeyo.

examples.romanization: sukjereul da hago naseo geimeul haesseoyo.
examples.en: I finished all my homework and then played games.

examples.ko: 이 영화를 보고 나서 책도 읽고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i yeonghwareul bogo naseo chaekdo ilkgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: After watching this movie, I want to read the book too.

commonMistakes: Using -고 나서 with an adjective; it needs an action verb because it implies finishing.
Adding tense before it, like 먹었고 나서; attach it to the plain stem and mark tense on the final verb.

after eating (I have to take medicine)

practiceItems.answer: 밥을 먹고 나서 약을 먹어야 해요.

practiceItems.answer: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 게임을 했어요.

studyOrder: Find the action you fully complete first
Attach -고 나서 to its plain stem
Keep that clause tenseless
Put the next action in the second clause, marking tense at the end
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-고 나서 tells the listener that you completely finish one action and only then start the next, putting a clear emphasis on completion. You attach -고 나서 to the plain verb stem with no changes, so 먹다 becomes 먹고 나서 and 씻다 becomes 씻고 나서, as in 손을 씻고 나서 밥을 먹어요 (I wash my hands and then eat). Because it implies finishing, it only works with action verbs, and you mark tense on the final verb, never as 먹었고 나서. It is worth comparing three similar tools: plain -고 simply lists actions in order, -고 나서 stresses that the first one is done, and -다가 means you broke off the first action partway to do the second. When the finish really matters, 고 나서 is the natural choice.

endingItems.title: Passive verbs (이/히/리/기)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Turns an action verb into a passive one, so the subject has something done to it instead of doing it.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when the focus is on what happens to the subject, not who does it — doors that open, things that get seen, food that gets eaten up. Very common in daily life and signs. Example: 문이 안 열려요. (The door won't open.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Insert one of -이-/-히-/-리-/-기- between the verb stem and the ending; which one is fixed per verb and must be memorized. -이-: 보다→보이다 (be seen), 놓다→놓이다, 쌓다→쌓이다. -히-: 닫다→닫히다 (be closed), 먹다→먹히다, 잡다→잡히다, 막다→막히다. -리-: 열다→열리다 (be opened), 듣다→들리다 (be heard), 팔다→팔리다, 밀다→밀리다. -기-: 안다→안기다, 끊다→끊기다, 쫓다→쫓기다, 씻다→씻기다. The agent, if mentioned, usually takes 에게/한테 (사람) or 에 (thing): 모기에게 물렸어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: 이/히/리/기 passive vs -아/어지다 passive: the four-marker type only works for a fixed set of transitive verbs and often describes a natural happening (문이 열렸어요 = the door opened/got opened), while -아/어지다 attaches more freely, often to describe a change of state or something becoming a certain way (이 펜은 글씨가 잘 써져요 = this pen writes well). Many verbs allow only one type.

examples.ko: 지하철에서 사람이 너무 많아서 문이 안 닫혀요.
examples.romanization: jihacheoreseo sarami neomu manaseo muni an datyeoyo.
examples.en: There are so many people on the subway that the door won't close.

examples.ko: 옆집 소리가 다 들려요, 벽이 너무 얇아요.
examples.romanization: yeopjip soriga da deullyeoyo, byeogi neomu yalbayo.
examples.en: I can hear everything from next door — the walls are way too thin.
It's a popular item, so it all sells out at lunchtime.
I got bitten on the leg by a mosquito yesterday.

commonMistakes: Guessing the marker — each verb takes a fixed one (열다→열리다, not 열이다; 닫다→닫히다, not 닫리다). They must be memorized verb by verb.
Using 을/를 with a passive verb. The thing affected becomes the subject with 이/가 (문을 열려요 ✗ → 문이 열려요 ✓).

practiceItems.prompt: Make 열다 (to open) passive, present polite: 'The window opens'
Make 닫다 (to close) passive: 'The door is closed'
Say 'I can hear music' using 듣다→들리다

studyOrder: Learn the four markers 이/히/리/기 as a set, then memorize a handful of high-frequency pairs (보이다, 닫히다, 열리다, 들리다, 팔리다).
Practice flipping the object to the subject: 문을 닫다 → 문이 닫히다.
Add the agent with 에게/한테 only when you really need to say who did it (모기한테 물렸어요).
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean passives slip a tiny syllable — 이, 히, 리, or 기 — inside the verb so the action happens TO the subject instead of being done BY it. So 닫다 (to close something) becomes 닫히다 (to be closed): 문이 닫혔어요 means the door got closed. The catch is that each verb is married to one specific marker, and there's no rule for guessing which — you just memorize them (열리다, 들리다, 보이다, 팔리다). You'll hear these constantly: 안 들려요 (I can't hear), 안 보여요 (I can't see), 다 팔렸어요 (it's all sold out). Start with those everyday ones and the pattern will click.

endingItems.title: Causative verbs (이/히/리/기/우)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Turns a verb into a causative one, meaning you make or let someone or something do the action.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you cause a change or make someone do something — feeding a child, waking someone up, lowering the price, raising the volume. Example: 아이한테 밥을 먹여요. (I feed the child rice.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Insert -이-/-히-/-리-/-기-/-우- between stem and ending; the choice is fixed per verb. -이-: 먹다→먹이다 (feed), 보다→보이다 (show), 죽다→죽이다, 끓다→끓이다. -히-: 입다→입히다 (dress someone), 앉다→앉히다 (seat), 눕다→눕히다, 읽다→읽히다. -리-: 살다→살리다 (save/keep alive), 울다→울리다 (make cry), 알다→알리다 (inform), 돌다→돌리다. -기-: 웃다→웃기다 (make laugh), 씻다→씻기다 (wash someone), 맡다→맡기다, 신다→신기다. -우-: 자다→재우다 (put to sleep; note 자→재), 서다→세우다 (stop/stand it up), 깨다→깨우다 (wake someone), 타다→태우다 (give a ride), 크다→키우다 (raise). The person made to act takes 에게/한테 or 을/를.
endingItems.contrastWith: Causative vs -게 하다: the embedded marker (먹이다 = feed directly) usually implies hands-on, direct causation, while V-게 하다 (먹게 하다 = make/let them eat) is more indirect — you cause it but they do the eating. 아이를 재우다 = I put the baby to sleep; 아이가 자게 하다 = I make the child go to sleep.
sentenceFrames: 소리/값을 ___ -여 주세요 (Please turn up / lower the ...)

examples.en: I'd just barely gotten the baby to sleep and the doorbell rang.
Driver, please stop at the next intersection.

examples.ko: 추우니까 아이한테 옷 좀 두껍게 입혀요.
examples.romanization: chuunikka aihante ot jom dukkeopge ipyeoyo.
examples.en: It's cold, so dress the kid in something thick.
I'm raising a puppy.

commonMistakes: Mixing up the look-alike passive and causative (보이다 can mean both 'be seen' and 'show'; 울리다 = make cry, but 울다 = cry). Context and particles tell them apart.
Forgetting the vowel shifts in the -우- group: 자다→재우다, 서다→세우다 (not 자우다, 서우다).

practiceItems.prompt: Make 먹다 (to eat) causative: 'I feed the baby'
Use 자다→재우다: 'I put the child to sleep' (past)
Use 서다→세우다: 'Please stop the car here'

studyOrder: Learn the five markers 이/히/리/기/우, then memorize the most useful pairs (먹이다, 입히다, 재우다, 깨우다, 세우다, 키우다).
Notice which causatives look identical to a passive (보이다, 울리다) and rely on particles to tell them apart.
Contrast the direct embedded causative with the looser V-게 하다 so you pick the right nuance.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Causatives add the same little syllables — 이, 히, 리, 기, or 우 — to mean you MAKE or HELP something happen. 먹다 (to eat) becomes 먹이다 (to feed): 아기한테 밥을 먹여요 means I feed the baby. The -우- ones change the vowel a bit, so 자다 (to sleep) becomes 재우다 (to put to sleep) and 서다 (to stand) becomes 세우다 (to stop/stand it up) — that 세워 주세요 is exactly how you tell a taxi to pull over. A few causatives look just like passives (보이다, 울리다), but the words around them make the meaning clear. Start with feed, dress, wake, raise, and stop — you'll use those all the time with kids, pets, and taxis.

endingItems.title: Do in advance & leave done (놓다/두다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Says you do something and leave it in that finished state, often as preparation for later.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you finish an action on purpose and leave the result standing — prepping ahead, keeping something ready, or leaving something as is. Example: 표는 미리 예매해 놓았어요. (I went ahead and booked the tickets in advance.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective (vowel harmony like the present tense) and add 놓다 or 두다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아 놓다/두다 (찾다→찾아 놓다, 사다→사 놓다); other vowels → -어 놓다/두다 (열다→열어 놓다, 만들다→만들어 두다); 하다 → 해 놓다/해 두다. Then conjugate 놓다/두다 freely (해 놨어요 from 놓았어요, 해 둘게요). In speech 해 놓다 often contracts to 해 놨어요. With a noun phrase you can also say 켜 놓다, 열어 두다, etc.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-아/어 놓다·두다 vs V-아/어 있다: 놓다/두다 keep an action's RESULT in place on purpose for later use (창문을 열어 놨어요 = I opened the window and left it open), while V-아/어 있다 just describes a state that exists (창문이 열려 있어요 = the window is (in the state of) open). 놓다 leans toward 'just did it / quick prep'; 두다 leans toward 'leave it for a while'.

examples.en: Guests are coming this weekend, so I made gimbap ahead of time.

examples.ko: 에어컨 켜 놓고 나왔는데 끄고 올걸 그랬어요.
examples.romanization: eeokeon kyeo noko nawanneunde kkeugo olgeol geuraesseoyo.
examples.en: I left the AC on when I went out — I should've turned it off.

examples.romanization: geu seoryuneun ildan chaeksang wie ollyeo duseyo.

Mixing it up with V-아/어 있다 for plain states — 'the window is open' is 열려 있어요, but 'I left it open (on purpose)' is 열어 놨어요.

Use 켜다 + 놓다: 'I'll leave the light on'

studyOrder: Build the -아/어 connective first (same as present tense), then bolt on 놓다 or 두다.
Practice contracting 놓았어요 → 놨어요, which is what you'll actually hear.
Feel the nuance: 놓다 = did it and it's ready now; 두다 = leave it sitting for later.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 놓다 and V-아/어 두다 both mean you do something and then leave it that way, usually to be ready later. Think prepping: 표를 예매해 놨어요 means I went ahead and booked the tickets. You make the -아/어 form (just like present tense) and add 놓다 or 두다, and in real speech 놓았어요 squishes to 놨어요. The two are nearly the same; 놓다 feels like you just did it and it's set, while 두다 feels like leaving it for a while. Don't confuse this with 열려 있어요 (the window is open as a state) — 열어 놨어요 means I opened it and left it open on purpose.

endingItems.title: While still in a state (-ㄴ 채로)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Means doing something while still in the state left by a previous action, often one you forgot to undo.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when one action's result is left in place while you do something else — sleeping with the lights on, going out with shoes on, talking with your mouth full. Often the state is a bit careless or unusual. Example: 불을 켠 채로 잤어요. (I slept with the lights on.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach to the PAST modifier form of a verb: vowel stem → -ㄴ 채로 (켜다→켠 채로, 신다... note 신다 is consonant), consonant stem → -은 채로 (신다→신은 채로, 입다→입은 채로). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ then add ㄴ (열다→연 채로). The 로 is optional — -(으)ㄴ 채 alone is also correct. It describes a maintained state, so the verb is usually one that leaves a lasting result (켜다, 입다, 신다, 열다, 앉다, 눕다). Not normally used with motion verbs like 가다.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 vs V-고: 신을 신고 들어갔어요 just sequences two actions (put on shoes, then went in), while 신을 신은 채로 들어갔어요 stresses that the shoes STAYED ON the whole time — often with a nuance of 'without taking them off', sometimes improperly. Also contrast with V-아/어서 (cause/sequence), which doesn't carry that 'left in that state' feeling.
sentenceFrames: ___(으)ㄴ 채로 자 버렸어요 (I fell asleep while still ___)

examples.ko: 어제 화장도 안 지운 채로 그냥 잤어요.

examples.romanization: sinbareul sineun chaero deureoomyeon an dwaeyo.

examples.romanization: changmuneul yeon chaero nawaseo jom geokjeongdwaeyo.
examples.en: I left with the window open, so I'm a bit worried.
I washed my face with my glasses still on.

commonMistakes: Using the present modifier instead of the past one — it's 켠 채로 / 신은 채로 (past form), never 켜는 채로.
Attaching it to adjectives or to plain motion (가는 채로 ✗). It needs a verb that leaves a lingering result-state.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 켜다: 'I slept with the TV on'
Use 신다: 'Don't come in with your shoes on'
Use 열다: 'I left with the door open'

studyOrder: Build the past modifier first (켜다→켠, 신다→신은), since 채로 always rides on that form.
Pick verbs that leave a state behind (입다, 신다, 켜다, 열다) and practice 'doing X while still in that state'.
Compare with V-고 to feel the difference between 'and then' and 'while still left that way'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄴ 채로 describes doing something while a previous action is still left in place — usually a slightly careless 'oops I didn't undo it' situation. 불을 켠 채로 잤어요 means I slept with the lights still on; 신발을 신은 채로 means with your shoes still on. The key is that it attaches to the PAST modifier form (켠, 신은, 연), not the present one. You drop it in when the state hangs around the whole time: makeup not removed, window left open, glasses still on. It's everyday and very natural — Koreans use it constantly to describe little forgetful moments.

endingItems.title: Special honorific words
endingItems.plainEnglish: A small set of completely different verbs you swap in to show respect, instead of just adding -(으)시-.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use with people you must honor — grandparents, parents, teachers, bosses, customers. Some lift the SUBJECT (계시다, 잡수시다), one lowers YOURSELF toward the listener (드리다). Example: 할머니께서 방에 계세요. (Grandmother is in the room.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Memorize these suppletive swaps. SUBJECT-honorific (honor the doer): 있다→계시다 (계세요), 먹다/마시다→드시다 or the higher 잡수시다 (잡수세요), 자다→주무시다, 말하다→말씀하시다, 아프다→편찮으시다, 죽다→돌아가시다. OBJECT/humble (lower yourself toward a senior): 주다→드리다 (드릴게요), 말하다→말씀드리다, 묻다→여쭤보다/여쭙다, 보다(meet)→뵙다/뵈다, 데리다→모시다. The honored subject also takes 께서 (이/가 honorific) and 께 (에게 honorific): 부모님께 선물을 드렸어요. 계시다 honors a person; for a respected person's possessions use 있으시다 (질문 있으세요?).
endingItems.contrastWith: Special words vs plain -(으)시-: most verbs just add -(으)시- (가다→가세요), but these high-frequency ones REPLACE the whole verb. Saying 있으세요 for a person is wrong where 계세요 is required (할머니가 계세요, not 할머니가 있으세요). And 드리다 is humble (you giving up), not honorific (someone giving to you), so a senior gives to you with 주시다, while you give to them with 드리다.
sentenceFrames: 할아버지께서 진지를 잡수세요 (Grandfather is eating his meal)

examples.ko: 사장님 지금 자리에 안 계세요. 메모 남겨 드릴까요?
examples.romanization: sajangnim jigeum jarie an gyeseyo. memo namgyeo deurilkkayo?

examples.romanization: naeil gyosunimeul boepgo yeojjwobol ge isseoyo.

commonMistakes: Using 있으세요 for a respected person who is present — for a person you must say 계세요 (있으시다 is only for their belongings/states, like 질문 있으세요?).
Using 드리다 when a senior gives to you. You receive from them with 주시다; 드리다 is only when YOU give to someone higher.

practiceItems.prompt: Say 'The teacher is in the office' honorifically (있다→계시다)
Say 'I'll give it to my parents' humbly (주다→드리다)

studyOrder: Memorize the swaps in pairs: 있다/계시다, 먹다/드시다·잡수시다, 자다/주무시다, 주다/드리다, 말하다/말씀드리다.
Learn the matching particles 께서 and 께, which travel with these honorific subjects and recipients.
Keep subject-honorific (계시다, 잡수시다) separate from humble (드리다, 뵙다) so you raise the right person.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: For most verbs you show respect by tucking in -(으)시-, but a handful of everyday verbs swap out entirely. 있다 becomes 계시다 when it's about a person (할머니가 계세요 = Grandma is here), 먹다 becomes 드시다 or the very polite 잡수시다, and 자다 becomes 주무시다. There's also a humble side: when YOU give something to someone above you, 주다 becomes 드리다 (부모님께 드릴게요). These come with their own particles, 께서 and 께. Two traps to remember: use 계세요 (not 있으세요) for a person who's present, and use 드리다 only when you're the one giving upward — when a senior gives to you, it's 주시다.

endingItems.title: Probably ... so (-ㄹ 텐데)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Expresses a strong guess or expectation, usually setting up a related comment, worry, or suggestion.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when you assume something is likely true and then add a thought based on it — concern, advice, or a contrast. Example: 길이 막힐 텐데 지하철로 갈까요? (It'll probably be jammed, so shall we take the subway?)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Built from -(으)ㄹ 터인데 (터 = expectation), almost always contracted to -(으)ㄹ 텐데. Vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 텐데 (바쁘다→바쁠 텐데, 오다→올 텐데, 멀다→멀 텐데), consonant stem → -을 텐데 (좋다→좋을 텐데, 먹다→먹을 텐데). PAST guess: -았/었을 텐데 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). NOUN: -일 텐데 (학생일 텐데). It can end a sentence as a soft 'I'd expect... (but)': 맛있을 텐데. With 1st-person intention it can also mean '(I) intend to ..., so' (나는 집에 갈 텐데).
endingItems.contrastWith: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 vs -(으)ㄹ 거예요: 거예요 just states a plain prediction (비가 올 거예요 = it'll rain), while 텐데 wraps that prediction in a 'so / but / I'm worried' frame that leads into another clause (비가 올 텐데 우산 챙겨요 = it'll probably rain, so take an umbrella). Also vs -(으)니까 (definite reason): 텐데 is a GUESS-based lead-in, softer and less certain.
sentenceFrames: ___(으)ㄹ 텐데 괜찮을까요? (It'll probably ___, will it be okay?)

examples.ko: 지금쯤 도착했을 텐데 왜 연락이 없지?
examples.romanization: jigeumjjeum dochakaesseul tende wae yeollagi eopsji?
examples.en: They should've arrived by now — why haven't they texted?

examples.romanization: jumarira saram maneul tende jom iljjing nagalkkayo?
examples.en: It's the weekend so it'll probably be crowded — shall we head out a bit early?
You must be hungry, so please at least have some of this.

examples.ko: 비 올 텐데 우산 안 가져가요?
examples.romanization: bi ol tende usan an gajyeogayo?
examples.en: It's probably going to rain — you're not taking an umbrella?

commonMistakes: Spelling it 텐대 — it's 텐데 (from 터인데).
Confusing the consonant/vowel split: 먹다→먹을 텐데 (not 먹ㄹ 텐데), 오다→올 텐데 (not 오을 텐데).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 막히다: 'The road will probably be jammed, so let's leave early'
Use 배고프다 + honorific: 'You must be hungry, so eat this'
Past guess with 도착하다: 'They've probably arrived already'

studyOrder: Start with present guesses (바쁠 텐데, 좋을 텐데) and add a worry or suggestion after them.
Add the past form -았/었을 텐데 for 'they've probably already ...'.
Compare with -(으)ㄹ 거예요 so you reserve 텐데 for guesses that lead into another remark.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: A/V-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is how you make a confident guess and then lean into a follow-up thought — worry, advice, or a gentle 'but'. 길이 막힐 텐데 means it'll probably be jammed, and you'd add something like 일찍 나가요 (so let's leave early). It comes from 터(expectation) + 인데, and you'll almost always hear the squished form 텐데. Use -을 텐데 after a consonant (먹을 텐데) and -ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel (올 텐데); for a past guess, add 았/었을 (도착했을 텐데 = they've probably arrived). It's warmer and more thoughtful than a flat 거예요, because it shows you're guessing and caring at the same time.

endingItems.title: Get done / become (-아/어지다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Makes a verb passive or shows a gradual change — something gets done, or a state comes about.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for things that happen on their own or get done without a clear doer, and for adjectives that gradually change. Example: 글씨가 잘 안 써져요. (The writing just won't come out / the pen won't write.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 지다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아지다 (작다→작아지다, 좋다→좋아지다), other vowels → -어지다 (만들다→만들어지다, 켜다→켜지다), 하다 → 해지다 (편하다→편해지다). With ADJECTIVES it means 'become/get more ~': 추워지다 (get colder), 많아지다 (increase). With some TRANSITIVE verbs it makes a passive of result: 켜다→켜지다 (get switched on), 깨다→깨지다 (get broken), 만들다→만들어지다 (get made), 쓰다→써지다 (get written). Conjugate 지다 normally (좋아졌어요, 깨졌어요).
endingItems.contrastWith: -아/어지다 vs 이/히/리/기 passive: -아/어지다 attaches very freely and often signals a CHANGE or a 'it just happens' feel (문이 잘 안 닫아져요... actually 닫히다 is preferred here), while the embedded-marker passive (닫히다, 열리다) is the lexical passive for a fixed verb set. For adjectives, only -아/어지다 works (날씨가 좋아졌어요 = the weather got better) — there's no 이/히/리/기 version.

examples.ko: 한국에 오래 살다 보니 한국말이 많이 편해졌어요.
examples.romanization: hanguge orae salda boni hangungmari mani pyeonhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After living in Korea a while, Korean has gotten a lot more comfortable for me.
I dropped my phone and the screen got cracked.
The weather suddenly got cold.
The light keeps turning off, it's a bit weird.

commonMistakes: Using -아/어지다 where a fixed lexical passive is standard (the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요).
Wrong connective vowel: 좋다→좋아지다 (not 좋어지다), 켜다→켜지다 (not 켜아지다).

practiceItems.prompt: Adjective change with 춥다: 'It got colder' (past)

studyOrder: Start with adjectives + 지다 to mean 'become more ~' (좋아지다, 추워지다, 많아지다).
Add the passive-of-result use on a few verbs (켜지다, 꺼지다, 깨지다, 써지다).
Compare with 이/히/리/기 so you know when the fixed lexical passive is the natural choice instead.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어지다 has two everyday jobs. With adjectives it means 'get/become more ~': 추워지다 is to get colder, 좋아지다 is to get better — 날씨가 추워졌어요 means the weather turned cold. With certain verbs it makes a passive that focuses on the result: 깨지다 (get broken), 꺼지다 (turn off), 켜지다 (turn on) — 컵이 깨졌어요 means the cup got broken. You just take the -아/어 form and add 지다. One thing to watch: some verbs already have a fixed passive (the door 'gets closed' is 닫혀요, not 닫아져요), so 아/어지다 isn't a free pass for every verb — but for adjectives turning into changes, it's exactly right.

endingItems.title: Come to / end up (-게 되다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Shows that something came about by circumstances rather than purely by your own choice.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when a situation leads to an outcome — you ended up doing something, came to feel a way, or things turned out so. Softens decisions so they don't sound boastful or blunt. Example: 회사 때문에 부산에서 살게 됐어요. (Because of work, I ended up living in Busan.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach -게 되다 directly to the plain verb stem with no vowel harmony (가다→가게 되다, 먹다→먹게 되다, 알다→알게 되다, 하다→하게 되다). Then conjugate 되다: most often past 게 됐어요 (= came to / ended up), also future 게 될 거예요 and present 게 돼요. ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ (살다→살게 되다). It pairs naturally with reasons like 덕분에, 때문에, 하다 보니까.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-게 되다 vs plain verb / -기로 하다: a plain 갔어요 just states you went; 가게 됐어요 frames it as 'it worked out that I went' (circumstances led there). And -기로 하다 is a deliberate decision YOU made (가기로 했어요 = I decided to go), whereas 가게 됐어요 downplays your agency. Korean often prefers 게 되다 to sound modest about good news (붙게 됐어요 = I ended up passing).

곧 ___게 될 거예요 (I'll come to ___ soon)

examples.romanization: chingu sogaero geu hoesae deureogage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Through a friend's introduction, I ended up joining that company.

examples.ko: 한국 드라마를 보다 보니까 한국어에 관심을 가지게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: hanguk deuramareul boda bonikka hangugeoe gwansimeul gajige dwaesseoyo.
