examples.romanization: sajeongi saenggyeoseo moime mot gage dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Something came up, so it turned out I can't make the gathering.

commonMistakes: Adding vowel harmony before 게 — it's just 먹게 되다, 가게 되다, never 먹어게 / 가아게.
Using it for a firmly chosen plan when you mean a decision; for 'I decided to', use -기로 했어요 instead.

practiceItems.prompt: Use 살다: 'I ended up living in Korea' (past)
Use 알다: 'I came to know him' (past)
Use 못 가다: 'It turns out I can't go'

studyOrder: Learn the past 게 됐어요 first — it's the workhorse 'ended up / came to' form.
Pair it with reason phrases (때문에, 덕분에, -다 보니까) that explain how it came about.
Contrast with -기로 하다 so you separate 'it worked out' from 'I decided'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-게 되다 says something came about because of circumstances, not just because you chose it. 한국에서 살게 됐어요 means I ended up living in Korea — maybe work or life pushed it that way. You attach -게 되다 straight to the stem (no vowel changes) and then usually use the past 게 됐어요. Koreans love this form for two reasons: it explains how a situation unfolded (덕분에 합격하게 됐어요 = thanks to you I ended up passing), and it sounds humble, since you're not bragging about your own decision. If you truly chose something on purpose, use 기로 했어요 instead; 게 됐어요 is for 'it turned out that...'.

endingItems.title: Resultant state (-아/어 있다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Describes the ongoing state that remains after an action is completed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use to say something stays in a finished condition — a door that's open, a person who's seated, a sign that's posted. The action already happened; you're describing the lingering result. Example: 의자에 앉아 있어요. (I'm (in a) seated (state).)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Take the -아/어 connective and add 있다: ㅏ/ㅗ stems → -아 있다 (앉다→앉아 있다, 남다→남아 있다), other vowels → -어 있다 (서다→서 있다, 열리다→열려 있다), 하다 verbs rarely use this. Works with INTRANSITIVE/result verbs and passives (가다→가 있다 = have gone and be there, 오다→와 있다, 죽다→죽어 있다, 켜지다→켜져 있다). For honor use 계시다 (앉아 계세요). NOTE: transitive 'be ~ing' is V-고 있다, not V-아/어 있다.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-아/어 있다 vs V-고 있다: 고 있다 = action in progress (문을 닫고 있어요 = I'm closing the door right now), while 아/어 있다 = the result-state after it's done (문이 닫혀 있어요 = the door is (already) closed). Also vs V-아/어 놓다: 놓다 stresses someone DID it and left it on purpose (문을 열어 놨어요), while 아/어 있다 just describes the existing state neutrally (문이 열려 있어요).

examples.en: A delivery has arrived (and is sitting) at the door.
It says 'under construction' on the wall.
Grandmother is (seated) on the sofa.

examples.ko: 불이 아직 켜져 있어요, 누가 있나 봐요.
examples.romanization: buri ajik kyeojyeo isseoyo, nuga inna bwayo.
examples.en: The light is still on — looks like someone's there.

commonMistakes: Using V-아/어 있다 with a plain transitive verb for 'be ~ing'. 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, never 읽어 있어요.
Wrong connective vowel: 앉다→앉아 있다 (not 앉어 있다); 서다→서 있다 (the 어 + 어 contracts).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 앉다: 'I'm seated on the chair'
Use 오다: 'A package has arrived (and is here)'

studyOrder: Lock in the contrast with V-고 있다 first: progress vs. resulting state.
Practice with verbs that leave a state: 앉다, 서다, 눕다, 오다, 열리다, 켜지다.
Swap 있다 for 계시다 when the person in that state deserves respect (앉아 계세요).
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-아/어 있다 describes the state that's left over after an action finishes. 앉아 있어요 doesn't mean you're in the act of sitting down — it means you're already (in the state of) seated. 문이 열려 있어요 means the door is open (someone opened it earlier and it stayed that way). The big thing to remember: this is NOT how you say 'be doing' — that's V-고 있다. So 'I'm reading' is 읽고 있어요, but 'the package has arrived and is here' is 와 있어요. Use 아/어 있다 with verbs that naturally leave a result hanging around: arrived, seated, standing, open, turned on. It's everywhere in descriptions of how things currently are.

endingItems.hangul: 안 V / V-지 않다 / 못 V / V-지 못하다
endingItems.romanization: an V / -ji anta / mot V / -ji mothada
endingItems.title: Negation: don't vs can't
endingItems.plainEnglish: Two ways to say no — 안/-지 않다 for simple negation, and 못/-지 못하다 for inability.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use 안/-지 않다 when you simply don't or won't do something, and 못/-지 못하다 when you can't because of ability or circumstances. Example: 오늘은 술 안 마셔요. (I'm not drinking today.) vs 운전 못 해요. (I can't drive.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: SHORT form: put 안 or 못 right before the verb/adjective (안 가요, 못 가요, 안 비싸요). For 하다 ACTION verbs the negator splits the noun and 하다: 공부 안 해요 / 공부 못 해요 (not 안 공부해요). LONG form: attach -지 않다 / -지 못하다 to the plain stem (가지 않아요, 가지 못해요, 좋지 않아요). 못 is for verbs only (ability), not for adjectives — for adjectives use 안/-지 않다 (안 예뻐요). NOTE the pronunciation: 못 해요 sounds like [모태요], 못 가요 like [몯까요].
endingItems.contrastWith: 안 (안 가요) vs 못 (못 가요): 안 = choose not to / simply don't (안 먹어요 = I don't eat it / I'm not eating); 못 = unable to (못 먹어요 = I can't eat it — allergy, too full, etc.). Short vs long form is mostly the same meaning; -지 않다/못하다 is a touch more formal or emphatic and is required in longer written sentences.
sentenceFrames: 오늘은 ___ 못 가요 (I can't go ___ today)

examples.en: I don't eat meat — I'm vegetarian.
I worked late yesterday, so I couldn't work out.
This restaurant isn't that expensive.
It's so spicy I really can't eat it.

commonMistakes: Putting 안/못 before the whole 하다 verb: it's 공부 안 해요 / 청소 못 해요, not 안 공부해요 / 못 청소해요.
Using 못 with an adjective. For 'not pretty' say 안 예뻐요 / 예쁘지 않아요 — 못 only negates ability of verbs.

practiceItems.prompt: Say 'I don't drink (alcohol)' with short 안
Say 'I can't drive' with short 못 (운전하다)
Say 'It's not expensive' with long form (비싸다)

studyOrder: Master the short forms 안 V and 못 V first — they're what you'll say out loud most.
Practice the 하다 split (운동 안 해요, 운동 못 해요), the most common mistake spot.
Add the long forms -지 않다 / -지 못하다 for writing and emphasis, and remember 못 is verbs-only.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has two flavors of 'no'. 안 (or the longer -지 않다) is plain negation: 안 가요 = I'm not going, 안 비싸요 = it's not expensive. 못 (or -지 못하다) means you CAN'T — you lack the ability or something blocks you: 못 가요 = I can't go, 운전 못 해요 = I can't drive. The classic trap is 하다 verbs: the 안/못 squeezes in between, so it's 공부 안 해요 and 운동 못 했어요, never 안 공부해요. One more rule: 못 is only for verbs (actions/ability), so 'not pretty' has to be 안 예뻐요, not 못 예뻐요. Get 안 vs 못 straight and your 'no' will sound natural right away.

endingItems.title: Almost happened (-ㄹ 뻔하다)
endingItems.plainEnglish: Says something nearly happened but didn't — a close call.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use for a near-miss, usually something bad you barely avoided: almost fell, almost forgot, almost late. Almost always in the past. Example: 길이 미끄러워서 넘어질 뻔했어요. (The road was slippery and I almost fell.)
endingItems.attachmentRule: Attach to the verb stem: vowel/ㄹ stem → -ㄹ 뻔하다 (넘어지다→넘어질 뻔하다, 울다→울 뻔하다), consonant stem → -을 뻔하다 (죽다→죽을 뻔하다, 늦다→늦을 뻔하다). It almost always appears as past 뻔했어요 (= almost did, but didn't). Used with action verbs about events, not with adjectives. Often paired with 하마터면 ... -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 (= 'I almost ...!'). 하다 verbs: 지각하다→지각할 뻔했어요.
endingItems.contrastWith: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 vs V-(으)ㄹ 것 같았다: 뻔하다 means it genuinely ALMOST happened (and clearly did NOT) — a real close call, while -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 is just 'it seemed like it would' (a guess/impression). 넘어질 뻔했어요 = I nearly fell; 넘어질 것 같았어요 = it felt like I was going to fall.
sentenceFrames: 큰일 ___(으)ㄹ 뻔했어요 (That almost turned into a disaster)

examples.ko: 하마터면 지하철에 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: hamateomyeon jihacheore gabangeul dugo naeril ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I almost left my bag on the subway and got off without it.

examples.ko: 차가 갑자기 튀어나와서 사고 날 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: chaga gapjagi twieonawaseo sago nal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: A car suddenly darted out and there was almost an accident.

examples.ko: 알람을 못 들어서 회사에 지각할 뻔했어요.
examples.romanization: allameul mot deureoseo hoesae jigakal ppeonhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I didn't hear my alarm and almost got to work late.
It was so moving I almost cried.

commonMistakes: Using the present 뻔해요 — a near-miss is finished, so it's almost always past 뻔했어요.
Wrong consonant/vowel split: 죽다→죽을 뻔했어요 (not 죽ㄹ), 넘어지다→넘어질 뻔했어요 (not 넘어지을).

practiceItems.prompt: Use 지각하다: 'I almost was late (for work/school)'
Use 잊다 with 하마터면: 'I almost forgot!'

studyOrder: Learn it straight in the past as 'almost ...ed but didn't' — 넘어질 뻔했어요.
Add 하마터면 in front for the natural 'I almost ...!' exclamation.
Contrast with -(으)ㄹ 것 같았다 so 'it really almost happened' stays separate from 'it seemed it would'.
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 is the 'I almost ___!' of Korean — a close call that, thankfully, didn't happen. 넘어질 뻔했어요 means I almost fell; 지각할 뻔했어요 means I almost got there late. Because a near-miss is already over, you'll basically always say it in the past as 뻔했어요. Pop 하마터면 in front to add drama: 하마터면 가방을 두고 내릴 뻔했어요 (I almost left my bag and got off!). Use -을 뻔했어요 after a consonant and -ㄹ 뻔했어요 after a vowel. It's super common in everyday storytelling about little disasters you dodged.

endingItems.title: Present Tense (Polite)
endingItems.plainEnglish: The everyday polite present tense — what is happening now or is generally true.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use V-아/어요 for almost everything in daily speech: current actions, habits, and general facts, e.g. 저는 커피를 마셔요 (I drink coffee). It is the safe default ending with most people.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 from the stem. If the last stem vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요 (좋다→좋아요). Otherwise add 어요 (먹다→먹어요, 읽다→읽어요). 하다 verbs become 해요 (공부하다→공부해요). Watch contractions: 가다→가요, 오다→와요, 마시다→마셔요, 주다→줘요, 보내다→보내요.
endingItems.contrastWith: The same stem rule builds the past tense — present 먹어요 (I eat) vs past 먹었어요 (I ate). Also don't confuse polite 아/어요 with casual 반말, which simply drops 요 (먹어, 가).

examples.en: I go to school every day.
My sibling is eating now.
On weekends I usually meet friends.
I study Korean.

commonMistakes: Adding 아요 after a non-ㅏ/ㅗ vowel, e.g. saying 먹아요 instead of the correct 먹어요.
Forgetting the contraction: saying 가아요 instead of 가요, or 마시어요 instead of 마셔요.
studyOrder: Drop 다 to find the stem
Check the last stem vowel: ㅏ/ㅗ takes 아요, everything else takes 어요
Apply 하다 → 해요 and watch for contractions (가요, 와요, 마셔요)
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The 아/어요 ending is the workhorse of Korean — the polite, everyday present tense you will use more than any other form. To build it, take the dictionary verb, drop 다, and look at the last vowel of what is left. If that vowel is the bright ㅏ or ㅗ you add 아요; for everything else you add 어요; and 하다 verbs turn into 해요. A few combinations squeeze together to be easier to say, so 가다 becomes 가요, not 가아요. Make 아/어요 your default and you will sound natural in almost any polite situation.

endingItems.title: Sino-Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The number set borrowed from Chinese — used for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, and most measured amounts.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use Sino-Korean numbers for dates (삼월 오일), money (오천 원), minutes (십 분), phone numbers, floors, bus numbers, and counting above 100. Example: 1,234 = 천이백삼십사.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 0 영/공, 1 일, 2 이, 3 삼, 4 사, 5 오, 6 육, 7 칠, 8 팔, 9 구, 10 십, 100 백, 1,000 천, 10,000 만, 억 (100 million). Build by place value: 23 = 이십삼 (2·10 + 3), 405 = 사백오, 30,000 = 삼만. Korean groups large numbers by 10,000 (만), not 1,000.
endingItems.contrastWith: Do NOT mix with native numbers (하나, 둘…). Money, dates, and minutes are always Sino; hours and counting objects are native. So 7:07 is 일곱(native) 시 칠(Sino) 분.

examples.en: Today is March 15th.
How much is this? It's 4,000 won.
My phone number is 010-2345...
The exam is in November.

commonMistakes: Saying 십천 for 10,000 — it is 만 (or 일만).
Reading minutes with native numbers — minutes are Sino: 삼십 분, not 서른 분.
Forgetting that 6 (육) nasalizes after ㄴ/ㅁ and in 육월 → it becomes 유월 for June.
studyOrder: Memorize 일~십 plus 백·천·만
Build tens and hundreds by place value
Practice dates, money, and minutes
Watch 만-grouping for big numbers
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has TWO number systems, and this is the 'Chinese-origin' one. You will use it constantly: every price, date, minute, and phone number is read with these. Learn 일 to 십 first, then 백 (100), 천 (1,000), 만 (10,000). To say bigger numbers you just stack place values: 이십삼 is literally 'two-ten-three' = 23. One surprise for English speakers: Korean counts big numbers in groups of 10,000 (만), so 30,000 is 삼만, not 'thirty-thousand'.

endingItems.title: Native Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The original Korean number set — used for counting things and people, ages, and the hour of the clock.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use native numbers to count objects (사과 세 개), people (두 명), animals (한 마리), age (스무 살), and hours (네 시). They are common from 1 to 99.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 하나 1, 둘 2, 셋 3, 넷 4, 다섯 5, 여섯 6, 일곱 7, 여덟 8, 아홉 9, 열 10; 스물 20, 서른 30, 마흔 40, 쉰 50, 예순 60, 일흔 70, 여든 80, 아흔 90. IMPORTANT: before a counter, 1–4 and 20 shorten: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. So 한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 살, 스무 살.
endingItems.contrastWith: vs Sino numbers (일, 이…). Hours use native (다섯 시) but minutes use Sino (오 분). Age uses native (스무 살); a year/date uses Sino. Above ~100, Korean switches to Sino.

examples.en: Three apples, please.
I am twenty years old.
It's four o'clock now.
I have two cats.

commonMistakes: Not shortening before a counter: it's 한 개 (not 하나 개) and 세 시 (not 셋 시).
Using native numbers for minutes or money — those are Sino.
Using Sino numbers for age or the hour — those are native.
studyOrder: Memorize 하나~열 then the tens 스물~아흔
Learn the four shorteners 한·두·세·네 (+스무)
Use for things, people, age, and hours
Switch to Sino above ~100
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is the 'home-grown' Korean number set, and the trickiest thing about it is that 1, 2, 3, 4 (and 20) change shape right before a counting word. You never say 하나 개 — you say 한 개. Memorize the four little shape-changers: 한, 두, 세, 네 (and 스무 for 20). You will use these for counting almost anything, for your age (스무 살), and for the hour on a clock (세 시 = three o'clock).

endingItems.title: Telling Time & Dates
endingItems.plainEnglish: How to read the clock and the calendar — which mixes BOTH number systems in one phrase.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use whenever you say a time or a date. The hour is a native number + 시; the minute is a Sino number + 분. Dates are Sino numbers + 년/월/일.
endingItems.attachmentRule: TIME: hour = NATIVE + 시, minute = SINO + 분. 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분. 3:30 = 세 시 삼십 분 (or 세 시 반, 'half'). DATE: year/month/day = SINO + 년/월/일. March 5 = 삼월 오일. Two month irregulars: June = 유월 (not 육월), October = 시월 (not 십월). Weekdays: 월·화·수·목·금·토·일 + 요일.
endingItems.contrastWith: The classic trap: in 일곱 시 칠 분, 시 takes a NATIVE number but 분 takes a SINO number — in the same breath. And 6월 = 유월, 10월 = 시월 each drop a sound.

examples.en: It's 7:07 now.
The meeting is at 2:30.
My birthday is June 10th.
Today is Friday.

commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 — the hour must be native: 일곱 시.
Saying 육월 or 십월 — June is 유월, October is 시월.
Using native numbers for the minute (it's 칠 분, not 일곱 분).
studyOrder: Hour = native + 시
Minute = Sino + 분
Dates = Sino + 월/일
Memorize 유월 & 시월
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Reading a clock in Korean is famously confusing because ONE phrase uses both number systems. The hour is a native number (일곱 시 = seven o'clock) and the minute right after it is a Sino number (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분 — same digit, two different words! Dates are all Sino (삼월 오일 = March 5). Just memorize two odd months: June is 유월 and October is 시월.

endingItems.title: Counters (Measure Words)
endingItems.plainEnglish: To count a noun you add a 'counter' word, like 'two CUPS of coffee' — and each counter picks native or Sino numbers.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use whenever you count a noun: NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER. 커피 두 잔 = two cups of coffee.
endingItems.attachmentRule: NATIVE-number counters: 개 (things), 명/분 (people; 분 is honorific), 마리 (animals), 살 (age), 시 (o'clock), 장 (sheets), 권 (books), 잔 (cups), 병 (bottles), 대 (cars/machines), 켤레 (pairs), 번 (times). SINO-number counters: 분 (minutes), 원 (money), 월/일/년 (date), 층 (floor), 호 (room), 인분 (food portions), 번 (number/order). Remember 1–4 shorten before native counters (한 개, 두 명, 세 잔).
endingItems.contrastWith: Watch the look-alikes: 분 = native 'people' (두 분) BUT Sino 'minutes' (이 분). 번 = native 'times' (세 번) BUT Sino 'order/number' (삼 번 버스).

examples.en: Two coffees, please.
I bought three tickets.
I have one puppy.
Three portions, please.

commonMistakes: Dropping the counter — Korean needs one: 사과 셋 → 사과 세 개.
Using the wrong number system for the counter (e.g., minutes are Sino).
Forgetting to shorten 하나/둘/셋/넷 before native counters.
studyOrder: Learn the pattern NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER
Learn which counters take native vs Sino
Memorize the most common: 개·명·마리·잔·장·번
Always shorten 한·두·세·네 before native counters
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: In English you can just say 'two coffees,' but Korean almost always slips a 'counter' word in: 커피 두 잔 (coffee two cups). Different nouns use different counters — 개 for general things, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups. The counter also decides whether the number is native or Sino. Start with the everyday ones (개, 명, 마리, 잔, 장) and remember the native numbers shrink in front: 한 개, 두 명, 세 잔.

endingItems.title: The (으) Rule: Consonant vs Vowel Stems
endingItems.plainEnglish: Dozens of endings add an extra 으 (or use 을/ㄹ) only when the stem ends in a consonant (받침).
endingItems.whenToUse: Apply it every time you attach an ending written with (으): -(으)면, -(으)세요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있다, -(으)ㄴ/ㄹ, -(으)니까, -(으)러, -(으)려고, -(으)ㄹ게요.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Look at the stem's last syllable. HAS a 받침 (consonant ending) → use the 으 form: 먹다 → 먹을 수 있다, 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹은. NO 받침 (vowel ending) → drop the 으: 가다 → 갈 수 있다, 가면, 가세요, 간. The 으 is just a helper so two consonants don't crash together. Exception: ㄹ-stems (살다) drop their ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings (사세요, 사니까, 삽니다).
endingItems.contrastWith: This is exactly the 갈 수 있다 (vowel stem 가-) vs 먹을 수 있다 (consonant stem 먹-) difference. Same ending, but 먹- needs the 으/을 helper and 가- does not.

examples.en: come → can come (vowel stem, no 으)
receive → can receive (consonant stem, +을)
see → if (you) see (vowel stem)
sit → if (you) sit (consonant stem, +으)

commonMistakes: Adding 으 to a vowel stem: 가으면 is wrong → 가면.
Dropping 으 from a consonant stem: 먹면 is wrong → 먹으면.
Forgetting ㄹ-stems are special: 살다 → 사세요 (the ㄹ disappears).
studyOrder: Find the stem (drop 다)
Check: does it end in a 받침?
Yes → add 으/을; No → skip the 으
Remember ㄹ-stem exceptions
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This one rule answers your 갈 수 vs 먹을 수 question — and it controls dozens of endings. When an ending is written with (으) in parentheses, you only use that 으 if the verb stem ends in a consonant (a 받침). 먹- ends in ㄱ, so you say 먹을 수 있어요 and 먹으면. 가- ends in a vowel, so you just say 갈 수 있어요 and 가면. Think of 으 as a tiny cushion that keeps two consonants from colliding. Master this and half of Korean conjugation suddenly makes sense.

endingItems.title: Liaison: Linking 받침 to the Next Vowel
endingItems.plainEnglish: A final consonant (받침) slides over to start the next syllable when that syllable begins with a vowel.
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens automatically in pronunciation whenever a 받침 is followed by a syllable that starts with ㅇ (a vowel sound).
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 + ㅇ-vowel → the 받침 becomes the next syllable's first sound. 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치, 한국어 like 한구거, 음악 like 으막, 옷을 like 오슬. With a double 받침, only the SECOND consonant moves over: 읽어 sounds like 일거.
endingItems.contrastWith: The spelling never changes — only the sound links. This is why 읽어요 (written) is pronounced 일거요. Learners who read block-by-block sound robotic; linking makes you sound natural.

examples.en: Korean language — sounds like 한구거
The flower is pretty — 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치
I read a book — sounds like 채글 일거요
I go home — 집에 sounds like 지베

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately (꽃#이) instead of linking to 꼬치.
Moving the wrong consonant in a double 받침 — only the second one links.
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by a ㅇ-vowel syllable
Slide the 받침 into that syllable
For double 받침, move only the second one
Read whole words, not block-by-block
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean words flow together. When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next one starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ), that consonant hops over and is pronounced at the start of the next syllable. So 한국어 is written in three blocks but sounds like 한구거, and 꽃이 sounds like 꼬치. The spelling stays put; only your mouth links them. This single habit is the biggest step from sounding like a textbook to sounding like a person.

endingItems.title: Nasalization
endingItems.plainEnglish: The stop sounds ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ turn into the nasal sounds ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ when followed by ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens automatically when a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침 meets a following ㄴ or ㅁ — extremely common in -습니다/-ㅂ니다 verbs.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: ㄱ(ㅋ,ㄲ) → ㅇ(ng); ㄷ(ㅅ,ㅆ,ㅈ,ㅊ,ㅌ) → ㄴ; ㅂ(ㅍ) → ㅁ. So 학년 → 항년, 입니다 → 임니다, 닫는 → 단는, 먹는 → 멍는, 끝나다 → 끈나다.
endingItems.contrastWith: Like liaison, it is a SOUND change only; spelling is unchanged. It's why polite 합니다 sounds like 함니다.

examples.en: Thank you — sounds like 감사함니다
Korean (language) — sounds like 한궁말
It ends — sounds like 끈나요
a person who eats — 먹는 sounds like 멍는

commonMistakes: Saying 학년 literally instead of 항년.
Missing it in -ㅂ니다/-습니다 endings (입니다 → 임니다).
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
Apply it to every -습니다/-ㅂ니다
Trust your ears over the spelling
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a 'hard stop' consonant (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ) bumps into a nasal sound (ㄴ or ㅁ), it 'goes nasal' to match: ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ. The most useful place to notice this is the polite ending: 합니다 is pronounced 함니다, and 입니다 is 임니다. It's the same reason 학년 (school year) sounds like 항년. You don't change the spelling — your mouth just smooths the two sounds together.

endingItems.title: Palatalization
endingItems.plainEnglish: A 받침 ㄷ or ㅌ becomes a ㅈ/ㅊ sound when the next syllable is 이 (or 히).
endingItems.whenToUse: It happens when ㄷ/ㅌ at the end of a stem meets 이 or 히 — common in 같이, 굳이, 붙이다, and 닫히다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (ji): 굳이 → 구지, 해돋이 → 해도지. ㅌ + 이 → 치 (chi): 같이 → 가치, 붙이다 → 부치다. ㄷ + 히 → 치: 닫히다 → 다치다. It only triggers before 이/히 — not before other vowels.
endingItems.contrastWith: Only before 이/히. 같이 is 가치, but 같아 is just 가타 (no change). This is why romanizing 같이 as 'gati' is wrong — it's gachi.

examples.en: Let's go together — 같이 sounds like 가치
You don't have to bother — 굳이 sounds like 구지
to stick a sticker — 붙이다 sounds like 부치다
the door closes — 닫히다 sounds like 다치다

commonMistakes: Saying 가티 for 같이 — it's 가치.
Applying it before other vowels: 같아 stays 가타, not 가차.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ/ㅌ 받침 right before 이 or 히
ㄷ→ㅈ(지), ㅌ→ㅊ(치)
Only before 이/히, no other vowel
Apply to 같이, 굳이, 붙이다…
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When a ㄷ or ㅌ at the end of a syllable runs into the vowel 이, your tongue is already near the roof of your mouth, so the sound shifts to ㅈ/ㅊ. That's why the very common word 같이 ('together') is pronounced 가치, not 'ga-ti.' Likewise 굳이 sounds like 구지. It only happens before 이 (or 히) — 같아 is still 가타. Once you know this, those 'why does it sound like that?' moments disappear.

endingItems.title: Aspiration
endingItems.plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to form the breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
endingItems.whenToUse: When a 받침 ㅎ meets ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ, or when a 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ meets ㅎ — common in 좋다, 축하, 못하다, 입학.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 ㅎ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅈ → ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅊ: 좋다 → 조타, 놓고 → 노코, 많지 → 만치. 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㅎ → aspirated: 축하 → 추카, 입학 → 이팍, 못하다 → 모타다, 백화점 → 배콰점.
endingItems.contrastWith: It's a merge, not a drop — the ㅎ doesn't vanish silently, it 'aspirates' the other consonant. So 좋다 is 조타 (with a strong t), not 조다.

examples.en: to be good — sounds like 조타
Congratulations — sounds like 추카해요
entrance exam — 입학 sounds like 이팍
I can't do it — 못해요 sounds like 모태요

commonMistakes: Saying 조다 for 좋다 — it's 조타.
Saying 축하 block-by-block instead of 추카.
studyOrder: Spot ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
They merge into ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ
Apply to 좋다, 축하, 못하다
Listen for the puff of air
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The letter ㅎ is friendly — it merges with a neighbor instead of staying separate. When ㅎ touches ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (in either order), the pair becomes one breathy consonant: ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ. So 좋다 is 조타, 축하 is 추카, and 못해요 is 모태요. The air 'puffs' out. This is why congratulations (축하) never sounds like 'chuk-ha' — it's 추카.

endingItems.title: Tensification
endingItems.plainEnglish: Plain consonants ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ become the tense ㄲ/ㄸ/ㅃ/ㅆ/ㅉ right after a stop 받침.
endingItems.whenToUse: After a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침, a following plain consonant tightens — very common in everyday words like 학교, 식당, 숙제.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 받침 ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ (and family) + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ → tense: 학교 → 학꾜, 먹다 → 먹따, 식당 → 식땅, 숙제 → 숙쩨, 입국 → 입꾹. It also appears after some ㄴ/ㄹ endings (갈게요 → 갈께요).
endingItems.contrastWith: Spelling shows the plain consonant, but you pronounce the tense one. 학교 is written with ㄱ but said with ㄲ (학꾜).

examples.en: I go to school — 학교 sounds like 학꾜
I eat at a restaurant — 식당 sounds like 식땅
Did you do the homework? — 숙제 sounds like 숙쩨
I'll go — 갈게요 sounds like 갈께요

commonMistakes: Saying a soft 학교 instead of the tense 학꾜.
Expecting the spelling to show ㄲ/ㄸ — it doesn't; only the sound is tense.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before a plain consonant
Tighten it: ㄱ→ㄲ, ㄷ→ㄸ, ㅂ→ㅃ, ㅅ→ㅆ, ㅈ→ㅉ
Apply to 학교, 식당, 숙제
Trust the sound, not the spelling
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: After a hard stop (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ at the end of a syllable), the next plain consonant gets 'squeezed' into a tense one. So 학교 sounds like 학꾜, 식당 like 식땅, and 숙제 like 숙쩨. The spelling still shows the soft consonant, but native speakers say the tense version automatically. You'll do it naturally once your ear gets used to it — for now, just know that 'school' is 학꾜, not a gentle 'hak-gyo.'

endingItems.title: Irregular Verb Types
endingItems.plainEnglish: Seven groups of verbs/adjectives whose stem changes before certain endings instead of staying fixed.
endingItems.whenToUse: Recognize the type from the stem's last letter, then apply its change when adding vowel endings like -아/어요 or -(으) endings.
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅂ-irregular: 덥다 → 더워요, 돕다 → 도와요. ㄷ-irregular: 듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요. ㅅ-irregular: 짓다 → 지어요, 낫다 → 나아요. 르-irregular: 빠르다 → 빨라요, 모르다 → 몰라요. ㅡ-drop: 쓰다 → 써요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요. ㄹ-irregular: 살다 → 살아요 but 사세요/삽니다 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ). ㅎ-irregular (adjectives): 빨갛다 → 빨개요, 어떻다 → 어때요.
endingItems.contrastWith: Regular verbs keep the stem (먹다 → 먹어요). Irregulars change it (듣다 → 들어요, not 듣어요). The trigger is usually a vowel ending; before consonant endings many stay regular.

examples.en: The weather is so hot. (ㅂ: 덥다→더워요)
I listen to music. (ㄷ: 듣다→들어요)
He's fast. (르: 빠르다→빨라요)
I write a letter. (ㅡ: 쓰다→써요)

commonMistakes: Treating an irregular like a regular: 듣어요 → it's 들어요.
Over-applying: not every ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ verb is irregular (받다 → 받아요 is regular).
Forgetting ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (살다 → 삽니다).
studyOrder: Identify the stem's last letter
Match it to one of the 7 irregular types
Apply the change before vowel endings
Memorize which common verbs are exceptions
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Most Korean verbs are predictable, but seven small groups bend their stem before certain endings. For example, ㄷ-verbs like 듣다 (to hear) turn the ㄷ into ㄹ before a vowel: 들어요, not 듣어요. ㅂ-verbs like 덥다 (hot) become 더워요. 르-verbs like 빠르다 (fast) become 빨라요. Don't try to memorize all at once — learn the type when you meet a common verb, and soon you'll feel the pattern. Watch out: not every verb that ends in ㅂ/ㄷ/ㅅ is irregular (받다 is regular: 받아요).

endingItems.title: Native Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The native number set (하나, 둘, 셋…) used to count things, people, animals, age, and the hour.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use native numbers to count objects, people, and animals, and to say age and o'clock: 사과 세 개 (three apples), 스무 살 (20 years old), 두 시 (two o'clock).
endingItems.attachmentRule: 1–4 and 20 change shape right before a counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 마리, 스무 살). From 5 up there is no change: 다섯 개, 열 명. Tens are their own words: 열(10), 스물(20), 서른(30), 마흔(40), 쉰(50), 예순(60), 일흔(70), 여든(80), 아흔(90). Native counting normally stops at 99; from 100 you switch to Sino 백.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼…), used for minutes, money, and dates. The clock mixes them: the HOUR is native (세 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (삼십 분).

examples.en: Three apples, please.
My younger sibling is ten years old.
I keep two cats.
I ordered four cups of coffee.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers to count objects — 사과 삼 개 is wrong; say 사과 세 개.
Forgetting the shape change: it is 두 개 (not 둘 개) and 스무 살 (not 스물 살).
studyOrder: Memorize 하나~열 first
Learn the 1–4 + 20 shape changes (한·두·세·네·스무)
Practice with the counters 개·명·살·시
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean has two number systems, and this is the 'native' one. You use it to count things you can see and touch, plus age and the hour on a clock. The tricky part: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 change to 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 right before a counting word — so 'two cups' is 두 잔, not 둘 잔. From 다섯 (five) on, nothing changes.

endingItems.title: Sino-Korean Numbers
endingItems.plainEnglish: The Chinese-derived number set (일, 이, 삼…) used for minutes, money, dates, phone numbers, and large numbers.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use Sino numbers for minutes (삼십 분), money (천 원), dates (3월 5일), phone numbers, floors, and counting from the hundreds up.
endingItems.attachmentRule: 일(1) 이(2) 삼(3) 사(4) 오(5) 육(6) 칠(7) 팔(8) 구(9) 십(10), then 백(100), 천(1,000), 만(10,000), 억(100,000,000). Combine the digits: 23 = 이십삼, 105 = 백오, 2024 = 이천이십사. Zero is 영 or 공 (공 in phone numbers). Sino numbers never change shape before a counter.
endingItems.contrastWith: Contrast with native numbers (하나, 둘…). The classic trap is the clock: the HOUR is native (일곱 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (칠 분), so 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분.

examples.en: This is 3,000 won.
Please wait just ten minutes.
My birthday is May 10th.
Take bus number 105.

commonMistakes: Reading minutes with native numbers — 삼십 분 is right, 서른 분 is wrong.
Forgetting that 6월 and 10월 are read 유월 and 시월 (not 육월/십월).
studyOrder: Memorize 일~십
Learn 백·천·만 and how to combine digits
Apply to money, minutes, and dates
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is the second number system, borrowed from Chinese. You use it for things you measure or label rather than count by hand: money, minutes, dates, phone numbers, and big numbers. Unlike native numbers, these never change shape. Watch the calendar: 6월 is 유월 and 10월 is 시월.

endingItems.hangul: 한 시 십 분 / 삼월 오일
endingItems.title: Telling Time & Dates
endingItems.plainEnglish: How to say clock times and calendar dates — which means mixing the two number systems.
endingItems.whenToUse: Use when telling the time (두 시 삼십 분 = 2:30) or giving a date (오월 오일 = May 5th, 금요일 = Friday).
endingItems.attachmentRule: TIME — the hour is a NATIVE number + 시 (한 시, 두 시 … 열두 시); the minute is a SINO number + 분 (오 분, 삼십 분). So 7:15 = 일곱 시 십오 분, and 'half past' is 반 (두 시 반). DATE — year, month, and day all use SINO + 년/월/일: 2024년 3월 5일 = 이천이십사 년 삼 월 오 일. Days of the week use 요일 (월요일, 화요일…). Note the irregular months: 6월 = 유월, 10월 = 시월.
endingItems.contrastWith: The hour is the ONE everyday time word that uses native numbers; minutes, dates, and years all use Sino. Mixing them up (일곱 분, 칠 시) is the most common beginner mistake.

examples.en: It's 7:07 now.
Class ends at 3:30.
My birthday is October 9th.
Today is Friday.

commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 (Sino) for 'seven o'clock' — the hour is native: 일곱 시.
Saying 일곱 분 (native) for minutes — minutes are Sino: 칠 분.
studyOrder: Hours = native number + 시
Minutes = Sino number + 분
Combine them: 일곱 시 칠 분
Dates = Sino + 월/일
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Telling time in Korean uses BOTH number systems at once, which surprises everyone. The hour is a native number + 시 (일곱 시 = seven o'clock), but the minute is a Sino number + 분 (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분. Dates are all Sino: 삼월 오일 (March 5). Just remember: hour = native, everything else = Sino.

endingItems.title: The (으) Insertion Rule
endingItems.plainEnglish: When a verb/adjective stem ends in a consonant, you add 으 before many endings; vowel-ending stems skip it.
endingItems.whenToUse: This runs through all of Korean. Whenever an ending is written with (으) — like (으)면, (으)세요, (으)ㄹ 수 있다, (으)러, (으)니까 — you choose the form by the stem's last sound: 먹으면 vs 가면, 먹을 수 있다 vs 갈 수 있다.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Drop 다 to get the stem. If the stem ends in a VOWEL (no 받침), use the short form: -면, -세요, -ㄹ, -러, -니까, -ㄴ (가면, 가세요, 갈, 가러, 가니까). If the stem ends in a CONSONANT (받침 있음), insert 으: -으면, -으세요, -을, -으러, -으니까, -은 (먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을, 먹으러, 먹으니까). ㄹ-final stems are special: the ㄹ stays for most endings (살면, 살아요) but DROPS before ㄴ/ㅂ/(으)-endings (살다 → 사세요, 사니까, 산).
endingItems.contrastWith: It is the SAME choice across many endings, so learn it once instead of memorizing each ending: 갈 거예요 / 먹을 거예요, 가면 / 먹으면, 가세요 / 먹으세요, 가니까 / 먹으니까.
sentenceFrames: (vowel) 가 + 면 → 가면   ·   (consonant) 먹 + 으면 → 먹으면
갈 수 있어요  ·  먹을 수 있어요

examples.en: Can I eat this?
If you go over there, it's there.
Please read slowly.
Let's go eat (in order to eat).

commonMistakes: Adding 으 after a vowel stem — 가으면 is wrong; it is 가면.
Forgetting 으 after a consonant stem — 먹면/먹세요 are wrong; it is 먹으면/먹으세요.
studyOrder: Find the stem (drop 다)
Check for a final consonant (받침)
Consonant → add 으 (먹으면); vowel → skip it (가면)
Watch ㄹ-stems: 살다 → 사세요
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: This is maybe THE most useful rule in Korean. Many endings are written with (으) in front — like (으)면 'if', (으)세요 'please', (으)ㄹ 수 있다 'can'. The 으 is just a little buffer vowel. If the verb stem ends in a consonant (먹-), add 으: 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을 수 있어요. If it ends in a vowel (가-), skip it: 가면, 가세요, 갈 수 있어요. Learn it once and it unlocks dozens of endings at the same time.

endingItems.title: Liaison — Linking Sounds (연음)
endingItems.plainEnglish: When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next starts with ㅇ (a vowel), that consonant slides over to begin the next syllable.
endingItems.whenToUse: This happens constantly in speech: 한국어 sounds like 한구거, 음악이 like 으마기, 꽃이 like 꼬치. The spelling never changes — only the sound links.
endingItems.attachmentRule: A final consonant (받침) before an ㅇ-initial syllable moves to become that syllable's onset: 꽃 + 이 → [꼬치], 음악 + 을 → [으마글], 옷 + 이 → [오시], 한국 + 어 → [한구거]. A double 받침 splits — one stays, one moves: 읽 + 어 → [일거], 앉 + 아 → [안자]. Liaison does not cross a clear pause between words.
endingItems.contrastWith: You still WRITE 꽃이, 음악을, 한국어 — only the pronunciation links. This is the #1 reason Korean sounds different from how it looks on the page.

examples.en: I study Korean. (sounds like 한구거)
The flowers are really pretty. (sounds like 꼬치)
I listen to music. (sounds like 으마글)
The clothes are too small. (sounds like 오시)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately (꼳-이 instead of 꼬치).
Forgetting a double 받침 splits: 읽어요 is [일거요], not [익어요].
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by ㅇ
Slide the 받침 into the next syllable
For double 받침, keep one and move one
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Korean is written in neat syllable blocks, but in speech a final consonant 'jumps' onto the next block when that block starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ). So 한국어 is read 한구거, and 꽃이 is read 꼬치. You keep spelling it the normal way — only the sound links up. Once you expect this, listening gets much easier.

endingItems.title: Nasalization (비음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: A stop consonant (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) turns into a nasal (ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ) when the next syllable starts with ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 감사합니다 sounds like 감사함니다 and 학년 like 항년. It happens whenever a stop 받침 bumps into ㄴ or ㅁ.
endingItems.attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: a ㄱ-type 받침 (ㄱㄲㅋㄳㄺ) → ㅇ (학년 → [항년], 국물 → [궁물]); a ㄷ-type 받침 (ㄷㅅㅆㅈㅊㅌㅎ) → ㄴ (받는 → [반는], 옛날 → [옌날]); a ㅂ-type 받침 (ㅂㅍㄼㄿ) → ㅁ (입니다 → [임니다], 앞문 → [암문]).
endingItems.contrastWith: Spelling stays the same (입니다, 학년). This is different from liaison: nasalization happens before ㄴ/ㅁ, while liaison happens before a vowel (ㅇ).

examples.en: Thank you. (sounds like 감사함니다)
I'm in third grade. (학년 sounds like 항년)
The broth is hot. (국물 sounds like 궁물)
This is Korean food. (입니다 sounds like 임니다)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing the hard 합니다 as written instead of [함니다].
Missing it in -습니다/-ㅂ니다 endings, which always nasalize to [-슴니다]/[-ㅁ니다].
studyOrder: Find a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
ㄱ→ㅇ, ㄷ→ㄴ, ㅂ→ㅁ
Apply it to every -ㅂ니다 ending
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: Some 받침 sounds soften when they run into ㄴ or ㅁ. A ㄱ-sound becomes ㅇ (학년 → 항년), a ㄷ-sound becomes ㄴ (받는 → 반는), and a ㅂ-sound becomes ㅁ (입니다 → 임니다). That's why the polite -습니다 ending is pronounced -슴니다. You don't change the spelling — just the sound.

endingItems.title: Palatalization (구개음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: A final ㄷ or ㅌ turns into ㅈ or ㅊ when the next sound is 이 (or 히).
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 같이 is pronounced 가치 and 굳이 is 구지. It only happens with ㄷ/ㅌ + 이.
endingItems.attachmentRule: When a 받침 ㄷ/ㅌ meets the vowel 이: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (굳이 → [구지], 해돋이 → [해도지], 맏이 → [마지]); ㅌ + 이 → 치 (같이 → [가치], 끝이 → [끄치], 붙이다 → [부치다]). With 히 it also applies: 닫히다 → [다치다].
endingItems.contrastWith: This is a special case of liaison: normally ㅌ + 이 would just link to [티], but before 이 the sound shifts forward in the mouth to [치]. Only ㄷ/ㅌ do this, and only before 이/히.

examples.en: Shall we go together? (같이 sounds like 가치)
You don't have to come (no need). (굳이 sounds like 구지)
I can't see the end. (끝이 sounds like 끄치)
I stick on a sticker. (붙여 area, 붙이- → 부치-)

commonMistakes: Reading 같이 as [가티] — before 이 it becomes [가치].
Over-applying it: it only affects ㄷ/ㅌ before 이/히, not other consonants or vowels.
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ or ㅌ 받침 right before 이/히
ㄷ → 지, ㅌ → 치
Remember the common word 같이 → 가치
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: When ㄷ or ㅌ at the end of a syllable meets 이, the sound slides forward and becomes ㅈ or ㅊ. So 같이 ('together') is said 가치, and 굳이 is 구지. It's a small rule, but 같이 is such a common word that getting it right (가치, not 가티) makes you sound much more natural.

endingItems.title: Aspiration (격음화)
endingItems.plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to make the strong, breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
endingItems.whenToUse: Why 좋다 sounds like 조타 and 축하해요 like 추카해요. It works in either order (ㅎ before or after the stop).
endingItems.attachmentRule: ㅎ + ㄱ (or ㄱ + ㅎ) → ㅋ: 축하 → [추카], 그렇게 → [그러케]. ㅎ + ㄷ → ㅌ: 좋다 → [조타], 많다 → [만타]. ㅎ + ㅂ → ㅍ: 입학 → [이팍], 잡히다 → [자피다]. ㅎ + ㅈ → ㅊ: 좋지 → [조치], 맞히다 → [마치다]. ㅅ-type 받침 + 해 also works: 못해 → [모태].
endingItems.contrastWith: The two plain sounds fuse into ONE aspirated sound — you don't hear ㅎ separately. Compare plain 다 vs aspirated 타 in 좋다 → [조타].

examples.en: The weather is really nice. (좋다 sounds like 조타)
Happy birthday! (축하 sounds like 추카)
I can't do that. (못해 sounds like 모태)
I entered university. (입학 sounds like 이팍)

commonMistakes: Trying to pronounce ㅎ as a separate sound — 좋다 is one fused [조타], not [조ㅎ다].
Missing it in 못해/안 해도 — 못해 is [모태].
studyOrder: Find a ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
Fuse them into ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ
Practice 좋다 → 조타 and 축하 → 추카
endingItems.beginnerExplanation: The letter ㅎ is 'breathy', and when it touches ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ, the two fuse into one strong aspirated sound: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ. So 좋다 is said 조타, 축하 is 추카, and 못해 is 모태. You won't hear the ㅎ on its own — it gets absorbed into the harder sound.
